speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will welcome the statement made by the Prime Minister with reference to the betterment of pension conditions for employees of the Canadian National Railways.
The Prime Minister correctly said that in 1959 there were important financial changes made with reference to the Canadian National Railways pension plan, as there were in a previous period, the date of which escapes me at the moment, when the predecessor of the present government was in office.
The Prime Minister was also right in saying that these matters are disposed of first and foremost by the Canadian National Railways pension plan board. This group comprises people who deal with the actuarial soundness of the pension plan of the Canadian National Railways. Unless my memory fails me at the moment there are approximately 15 or 20 members representative of the various railway unions and of the various divisions of the operating branches of the Canadian National Railways.
The Prime Minister was also quite right in saying that the matter had been submitted to the sessional committee on air lines and other agencies owned and operated by the government, which committee had heard evidence on the matter. I am sure the house will remember also that representations had been made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) to the committee and the house on many occasions with reference to the betterment of conditions concerning this pension plan.
While I have no right to introduce a contentious note, and have no intention of doing so, I would remind the house and the Prime Minister that these matters might well have been disposed of a long time ago. It could well have been done by the sessional committee or on recommendation from them. It might well have been done much earlier in the session by a bylaw passed by the Canadian National Railways, which is now tabled. This government has been in office now over 4J years and could have done it at a prior time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN PENSION PLAN
speechtext: What about the previous 22 years?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
However, that does not derogate from the fact that these recommendations as put forward to the Prime Minister by the Canadian National Railways pension board are excellent and commendable, and


the house and the country I am sure will accept them with satisfaction. However, I would add this comment. It is unfortunate that the government has not thought of coming to the assistance of the railway workers, some 25,000 of them, who have been put out of work by the policies of the present government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN PENSION PLAN
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is departing from the subject matter of the announcement. I recognize the hon. member for Port Arthur.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everybody seems to be a lion this morning for the poor railway worker. It seems to me, if I correctly caught the Prime Minister's phrasing that this announcement applies only to existing employees rather than to existing employees and existing pensioners. If that is the case there will be considerable disappointment. If he reviews the proceedings of our committee last year, he may remember that the main impetus for a review came from the people who were presently on pension. This organization is centred in Winnipeg. The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) had arranged for them to speak at the committee hearing. They made their presentation to all of us. I know that, even as the Prime Minister suggests, there will be considerable disappointment, and this notwithstanding the fact that the present employees of the Canadian National Railways will be delighted from their point of view. If I am wrong in this assumption I hope the Prime Minister will correct me.
However, it seems to me there is almost an unexpected turn here in view of the opinion expressed last year by the president of the C.N.R. before our committee that it was most unlikely that the pension board or the management could see their way clear to improve the pensions. The question, of course, that will remain in our minds extends not only toward the existing pensioners but also toward the fact that the very same conditions that created a poor pension period for the workers on the Canadian National Railway also apply to the other giant railway.

Last night before the committee rose there was some discussion which had to be cut off with regard to the work being done by the queen's printer in connection with the printing and distribution of the Canadian Bill of Rights. We in this party feel that the bill of rights was probably one of the proudest achievements which parliament has been able to carry out over


the past century. However, I think the worst thing which could be done is to associate this achievement with any particular party or prime minister.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: On a point of order, would the hon. member indicate if it is not our Prime Minister and the Conservative party who should be given any credit for it? The Liberals opposed it for 22 years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

It is obvious that what the minister has said is right. This is something which was introduced into this house by the Prime Minister, but surely it was passed by this parliament and endorsed by all the members of the other parties. When such a document is being published at public expense I think it would be better understood if it were not partisan.
This is by no means the first bill of rights which has been drawn up. There is, for example, the constitution of the United States of America. The reason this receives the respect of all people is that it is non-political; no political party has made it a special area of concern.
I wonder if the hon. member would feel that the children in the United States reciting the Gettysburg address are participating in a partisan activity?
Surely not; but I have no knowledge that the government of the United States produces copies of the Gettysburg address at the public expense and sends them out to the school children.
They do.

This document must surely be looked upon with approval by Liberals and by members of the New Democratic party. It must be capable of being hung in the homes of all people. It must be capable of being hung in school rooms and looked upon with pride by people belonging to all parties and of all persuasions. I would hope, therefore, that the queen's printer would change the format which has been used.
Some days ago I placed a question on the order paper in relation to the use which is being made of the bill of rights. In one supermarket in Toronto copies were being dispensed as part of a promotion campaign for selling toothpaste. I am not going to blame the government for this, and I am not sure that the format used by the queen's printer was being used in this instance. Surely if we want this document to receive the respect of people of all political persuasions we do

not want the name of any political personage on it. That should be the rule of thumb with regard to all such documents when they are produced at public expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Last night we heard a statement from the hon. member for Leeds concerning a particular document published by the queen's printer bearing the signature of the Prime Minister in relation to the enactment by parliament of the bill of rights. The hon. member for Peterborough has proceeded this morning to add his contribution to the most extraordinary statement made last evening by the hon. member for Leeds. The hon. member for Leeds is new and he may be very gullible but he should not, I think, attempt to go very much further in his political career making the kind of statement he made last night unless he has checked his facts first. The hon. member will find it is a good practice to check facts before assertions are made in this House of Commons, and I commend the same advice to the hon. member for Peterborough.
I wish to make two points in relation to this matter. We are speaking here of a document printed by the queen's printer and made available by him to the public. I wish to speak first of all of the commercial aspects of the matter; then I wish to deal specifically with the objections taken by these hon. members to the use of the signature of the Prime Minister on a government publication.
The first fact that 1 think is worthy of the attention of the committee is that this is not a publication that is costing the taxpayers of Canada so much as one cent. The hon. member for Leeds put this matter before the committee last evening as though public funds were being used in an improper manner with a view to publicizing the photograph and signature of the Prime Minister. Surely the hon. member does not object to the assertion that the Prime Minister introduced the bill of rights in this house.
With the help of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With no help from the Liberal opposition, Mr. Chairman; none whatever. Of course it was parliament that enacted the bill of rights; only parliament could. During 22 years in office hon. members opposite had not only made no effort to introduce a bill of rights but they had opposed efforts made by the present Prime Minister when he was in opposition to introduce and enact a bill of rights. When the Prime Minister in 1960 introduced the measure to enact the bill of rights in this country, was there any assistance from hon. members opposite? No, there was not, Mr. Chairman.

Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If hon. members opposite are prepared to admit that the records of this house are correct in indicating that the Prime Minister introduced the bill to enact the Canadian Bill of Rights, then perhaps we may now move on to consider the question whether public funds are being used at all in this matter, let alone used in some improper way to give currency to the photograph or signature of the Prime Minister in some manner that is not proper. The fact is that the treasury is making money on this publication; it is a best seller. It costs 30 cents to print every copy of this publication, and we are selling it at $1 a copy. We are not giving it away. We are not imposing a burden on the treasury. We are selling this publication and making a handsome profit on every sale.

Turning now to point No. 2, is there something extraordinary about the use of the signature or photograph of the Prime Minister on a publication? To listen to the hon. member for Peterborough talk, any document that bears the name of a minister in office obviously is immediately disqualified because he is a political figure.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is going to have to revolutionize the practice that has existed here in parliament for many and many a year, because documents issued under the authority of a minister must be so described. They do not just come out without some authorization and it is customary, of course, on all these documents to name the source of authority. If that were not given, of course, hon. members opposite like the hon. member for Peterborough would be screaming about there being no shown source of authorization.
What are the facts here? It was a new member who was chosen by the Liberal party to make such a foolish, uninformed and misleading statement last evening. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who always rises and tells us he does not remem-

What are some of the facts the hon. member for Leeds evidently was not aware of and had not taken the trouble to find out, and which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate had either forgotten or did not choose at the time to bring to the attention of the hon. member for Leeds before that hon. gentleman got himself any further into the posture of putting his foot in his mouth?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What are the facts? Let me turn up just a few publications. The hon. member for Leeds is a Liberal; he was elected as a Liberal. I have before me a government publication entitled "Canada-1949". This is a government publication issued when the Liberals were in office. What do I find? Here is an insert entitled "A Message from the Prime Minister of Canada".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This message was printed, Mr. Chairman, and it bears the signature "Louis S. St. Laurent, Prime Minister". The document is dated January 1, 1949. Fifty thousand copies of this document were printed. I suppose those 50,000 signatures must be a very great burden upon the soul and conscience of the hon. member for Leeds. They have been in existence for the last 13 years. The publication contains a message from the prime minister of that day. He tells the story of the entry of Newfoundland into confederation. I suppose on the theory that he was a political figure the hon. members for Leeds and Peterborough would say it is highly improper that a message of this kind accompanying a government publication should have borne the signature of the prime minister of Canada.
A different situation altogether.

Would the Minister of Finance permit a question? Am I correct in assuming that that particular publication would have been printed at public expense, unlike the document that is presently being discussed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Leeds may perhaps draw a distinction between documents bearing the signature of a prime minister and documents bearing a photograph of a prime minister. Let us see what we have here. I have in my hand another publication entitled "Canada-1948".

I have shown this photograph to the committee and pointed out that it is a very expensive printing job because it is all in colour. Anyone who knows anything about printing knows that the addition of colour makes a printing job very much more expensive. Although much additional money was spent on printing that photograph in colour, this publication still sold at the same low price of 25 cents.

What about the content of the message? It may be significant in testing whether there is any political aspect to such a publication or political advantage to the prime minister of the day if we examine the printed matter that accompanied this handsome coloured reproduction of the photograph of the prime minister in 1948. What this is all about is not an announcement of Newfoundland entering confederation. It is not an announcement of the enactment of a very important constitutional document on the government of Canada. This printed matter contains, if you please, the record in office of the then prime minister, in 1948, namely Mr. King. It purports to tell the story-of course in the same glowing terms-of the length of time he had been in office, and it compares him with some other lesser prime ministers who had not survived in office quite so long. If this has no political aspect to it, or if there was no political value accruing therefrom to the prime minister of the day or to the party he led at the time, then I am a very innocent person indeed. However, I must confess to having not only the deep suspicion but the profound conviction that this particular page appearing in this publication opposite the photograph of the prime minister had the effect of painting his record in glowing terms, just as did his photograph appearing in colour.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. My point of order is that the hon. member is trying to mislead the committee by suggesting that the Prime Minister signed the act, whereas on this illuminated copy of the bill of rights the Prime Minister's signature appears under a quotation and not under the act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am afraid the hon. member is engaging in debate and not raising a point of order.

I do not quite understand why the hon. member rose, but because of the point he mentioned I am going to ask this question. Do hon. members think that in any publication of the statute we should have not only the statute but a quotation from Hansard and the document signed by the prime minister of a Conservative government or any other government?
Is it signed in the statute book?

This is a most unusual procedure. I say this is not a matter of putting forward the principles of the bill of rights. It is strictly a campaign approach, and I say that it brings this House of Commons and the other place into disrespect that this kind of thing should be used for political purposes and should not be a matter of principle and of right acceptable to all parties and all people, as the Prime Minister told us it would be when he introduced the bill of rights.
I want to come back to what I was saying when I was interrupted. If this document has

been produced in the form it has been because of the great principles embodied in the bill of rights, I say it is very peculiar that the Minister of Finance did not see fit to go beyond stating that this was a matter which had been deep in the heart of the present Prime Minister ever since he entered the House of Commons as a member of the opposition and mention also that over 30 years ago Rev. J. S. Woodsworth fought for a bill of rights from the very day he entered this house, and so did M. J. Coldwell, who is no longer with us. Neither the Liberals nor the Tories would accept a bill of rights when it was demanded over 30 years ago, but we are very happy that finally they did repent.
You mean the Liberals.

My only regret is that the bill of rights now on the statute books of Canada is being used for political purposes and not as a statute of principles. I also regret that it was not made an irrevocable part of the constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, whether that act remains a statute of the British parliament or whether our constitution is brought home to Canada where it belongs. The bill of rights is something that should mean a great deal to all citizens, and it should not be used for political expediency by a government that does not know how to be elected except by using misleading propaganda and misusing a statute of the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, much has been made of this signature on the bill of rights, but what I am proud of and pleased about is that this name of Diefenbaker is not only on the bill of rights but is inscribed in the hearts of the members of every ethnic group in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say this. When we hear the hon. member for Vancouver East stand up here and talk about the rights of people, after his party used a technical procedure of the house yesterday to deprive individuals of rights that they are guaranteed under the laws of this country, I do not think it goes down very well.
Mr. Chairman-

Hansard speaks for itself. Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the committee too much, and I am going to turn from this matter which is relatively controversial. I would ask the Minister of Finance to draw the attention of the queen's printer to the importance of expediting the printing of the statutes of Canada. speechtext: That expression is no better. It is equally an offence against the rules of parliament to say that an hon. member uses fascist tactics.

speechtext: It cannot be applied to an hon. member of the house. It is quite clear that it is unparliamentary and I ask you, sir, to require the hon. member to withdraw it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To my mind the term is unparliamentary, and I am sure the hon. member would not want to persist in using it.

I think the tactics are such, but I will be pleased to withdraw it if it offends the Chair.
We were discussing the printing of the bill of rights the other night, and I believe the minister failed to mention something that should be mentioned in this regard. I believe all Canadians are pleased that this particular document has been put out and that there is a bill of rights, although we all know the act does not go far enough. We also know that by putting in this signed statement from Hansard a complete false impression is being given. If this statement from Hansard had been separated from the extract from the bill there would be some justification for it.
I believe that Canadian students across the country are going to be more interested in this than anyone else. However, the document does not contain the whole of the bill of rights. The bill of rights has two parts, and it might be of interest to hon. members to know what the other part of the bill of rights says because it might have some bearing upon whether or not the statement by the Prime Minister is applicable. Section 5 (2) of part II reads as follows:
The expression "law of Canada" in part I means an act of the parliament of Canada enacted before or after the coming into force of this act, any order, rule or regulation thereunder, and any law in force in Canada or in any part of Canada at the commencement of this act that is subject to be repealed, abolished, or altered by the parliament of Canada.
Obviously this section gives to the parliament of Canada responsibility for the administration of this act, not the prime 

minister of the country. The third paragraph of section 5 reads:
The provisions of part X shall be construed as extending only to matters coming within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.
The following section refers to the War Measures Act, and the remainder of the act occupies almost as much space as the printed document to which I referred. At the end of the act we find the words "The Queen's Printer and Controller of Stationery, Ottawa, 1960." This act, as contained in the statute books, is not signed by the Prime Minister. The Minister of Finance, I was surprised to hear, said this was a very good piece of literature to be distributed by the queen's printer because it cost 30 cents and sold for $1. Well, sin pays too, but we do not necessarily sell it merely because one can make a profit on it. I do not think this is a reason for having this document printed and sent out. I feel that the complete bill of rights should be sent to the children of this country simply because we want them to learn what is contained in the bill of rights, and what protection is afforded by it.
It would have been far better, therefore, if the Prime Minister had the whole act printed. Perhaps this would have stimulated a desire on the part of the children to extend the bill of rights and make it constitutional rather than the statutory type of act which it is now. This is not a constitutional document and is not in the same category as the bill of rights of the United States. I believe this document is being misinterpreted when it is published in this manner. This scorn should not be heaped on the opposition because we want to be more factual_____
That will be a change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is he not aware that it is the first part of the statute that is known as the bill of rights, and is so described in the statute itself?
Chapter 44 starts out with the preamble to which we have already referred. Part I is the bill of rights, and part II has no designation at all, it is just headed "Part II".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What is the last section, at the end?

Section 4 reads:
The provisions of this part shall be known as the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Oh, oh.

Here are these lawyers arguing about something that is really not correct. I grant that the short title for this part I is "The Canadian Bill of Rights", but part II is not separated in any way from part I. I suppose there is a technicality here, but I am not a lawyer. Both hon. members who are questioning this are lawyers. Would they consider this to be a legal document? Could a layman look at this and say "This is my bill of rights and I am going to take this document into court with me"? This document cannot be presented in court. Is this not true? I ask the Minister of Finance, who is a qualified lawyer, if this document has any legal status in court?
Who said it had?
Nobody said it had; I am just asking the question.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Is anyone going to say that I can take this document into court and present it as the bill of rights? If I took this into court, I would be thrown out.
True.

It only becomes propaganda, therefore, and it is this to which we are objecting. If the complete act had been printed it would have covered only one more column in this illuminated document and then I could take this document into court, even with the illumination. It is the propaganda aspect of the matter to which we are objecting.

I should like to speak to the point raised by the hon. member. I suggest that even if the complete bill of rights were reprinted, as he has suggested, on a piece of paper it would still not be recognized by courts of law. He would have to produce the statutes of Canada in court, and they would be recognized. There has been a practice of reprinting excerpts of statutes, such as Magna Carta, but when you go into a court of law you rely on the complete statute. Nobody is being misled. There is a reference at the top to the statutes of Canada, and if the school children are as interested as the hon. member thinks, then it is quite easy for them to get a copy of the statute and read the whole thing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this particular subject because I think there is a basic principle involved here that has been completely overlooked, not only in this particular incident but in a lot of other incidents that have been occurring recently. The Prime Minister of this country is the head of a political party,
Supply-Secretary of State and he always has been. When the opposition comes along and says that because the name of the Prime Minister is appended to a certain document it is therefore a political document, they are just quibbling and quibbling shamefully. I can assure hon. gentlemen that there are a good many people in this country-and in fact they will soon learn they are a majority of the people of this country-who regard the prime minister-our present Prime Minister-as the leader and head of this country. They believe that the Prime Minister and the office of prime minister deserve the respect of the people of this country.
I feel that this principle has been bypassed for the sake of political expediency and an effort has been made to bring down the Prime Minister of this country to a level to which he should not be brought down. The Minister of Finance gave many examples of this type of thing. It is absolutely impossible to say that this government is not run by political figures, because they are and we all know it.
There have been a good many examples of this sort of thing in the last two years. I refer to trying to drag down the head of this country, and the government in general as far as that goes, for political purposes in order to attempt to degrade this government and this country in the eyes of other people.
I say this is not the feeling of the people of Canada. The people of Canada want to respect, and they do respect, the Prime Minister of the country while he holds office. I think it will be shown very shortly that the present Prime Minister does hold the respect and confidence of the people as prime minister of this country. I think all the things that have been said in this debate have been directed at one thing only. The opposition say this is a political document. If there is any vestige of truth in that statement it is not one tenth the amount of political dragging down that has been carried out in regard to this particular issue.
We are all proud of the bill of rights. I have gone into schools and have been shown the bill of rights hanging up, with the Prime Minister's signature on it. It was held in more respect because there was a signature to it. There is a living person, the Prime Minister, attesting to this document; it is not just a cold statute of Canada. The people of this country know, as has already been said today, that this has been a project of the Prime Minister for a long time. I say there is nothing more than a political effort and a great deal of quibbling in this whole argument. I think it does not help the position of parliament to raise this matter in a political manner in an effort to discredit the Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a very few words on this subject. To allege that the document the hon. member has on his desk is a political document is, in my view, the same as alleging that any reproduction of the Gettysburg address by Abraham Lincoln amounts to a political document in support of the Republican party in the country to the south.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka in everything he said. I think we all have respect for our Prime Minister as prime minister, and this has to be kept on a level where it is respect for the head of the country, no matter who the particular head may be. I think it is very difficult to keep this idea separated in Canada. We know this. We have to elect our prime minister, in our political set-up; therefore it becomes more and more difficult to make the separation.
I am very concerned about this matter of the Canadian Bill of Rights. When we went to school as children I am sure everybody in this country felt we should have something more, because of the fact that we were only a dominion to start with, to which we could tie our Canadian citizenship. For this reason I believe the hon. member will agree with me that regarding the Canadian Bill of Rights, while you can put in one comer the illumination that is already there, it should be in the form of illumination and the bill of rights itself should be complete so it may be the charter of Canadian citizenship, the rights of Canadians as Canadians. There is no objection to the fact that the present Prime Minister introduced this bill of rights, and we all give him credit for having been interested in it for a long time; but when we have the queen's printer printing it, it should be in terms of illumination rather than just a part of the document. This is my point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are just one or two brief statements I should like to make in connection with this matter. In view of the fact that the parties to the dispute between the pilots and the shipping federation of Canada are now meeting, I will make my remarks as brief as possible.
I would like to make several points rapidly; first, the importance of settling this dispute as quickly as possible because of the damage it has caused and will cause to the Canadian economy if it is allowed to go on much longer; second, because of the inconvenience it is causing to the travelling public; and last but not least, the danger to the safety of navigation. This danger to navigation has been demonstrated by the ship Eskimo which got into difficulties a few miles outside the port of Montreal because it was navigating without a pilot, and also by the Consuelo, a British ship which tangled with an anchor in the port of Quebec; the anchor hooked up the cables telecommunication services and caused substantial damage.
It is also important that this strike be not allowed to go on because of the fact that navigation is opening on the St. Lawrence seaway; that is, upstream from Montreal. This opening has been announced for April 15. If settlement is not forthcoming by that

time, tremendous damage will ensue. In that area ships must have pilots. Pilotage is compulsory in accordance with section 375(b) of an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, though much to my surprise yesterday, when I told the Minister of Transport that from St. Regis in the province of Quebec upstream there was an obligation on the part of shipping to have compulsory pilotage, his reply was that St. Regis was not on the St. Lawrence river. Of course, to anyone who knows the St. Lawrence there is no doubt that it is.
Then again, there is the reasonable suggestion which has been put forward from time to time that a public inquiry should be undertaken. Five grievances of the pilots have been submitted to the minister, two of which have already been granted. It seems to me that the remaining three points could be settled were an undertaking given by the ministry of transport that a public inquiry would be held to consider the whole subject of pilotage.
I appreciate that there are difficult problems which arise in the Department of Transport in connection with these matters. It has been my feeling all along that while under the Canada Shipping Act the pilots are subject to the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport, when a dispute of this kind arises it might be determined not by the Minister of Transport but by the minister whose responsibility it is to deal with such matters, namely the Minister of Labour. I make that suggestion without the slightest reflection on the Minister of Transport. When I was in the Department of Transport I often wondered why it was that the Minister of Transport as the pilotage authority should have the responsibility for settling stoppages of this kind. I am wondering if the Canada Shipping Act should not be amended so that when there is a dispute of this kind, or when pilots holding meetings and the federation refusing to meet with them, the Minister of Labour should enter the picture.
I hope there will a settlement of the dispute, and I trust that the parties will agree to a public inquiry under the direction of the government so that all aspects of this pilotage question may be explored insofar as they concern the pilots, the ship owners and the ship operators. If this were done a great service would be rendered to an important branch of our economy.

conditions in the field of railways and railway operations, the fixed charges of the C.N.R. have been increasing over the years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a known fact that employment on the railways has been declining. Broadly speaking, I think there are two reasons for this fact. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall try to be as brief as possible on this item, Mr. Chairman. However the minister gave me an entree to discuss it when a moment ago on item No. 752 he said that the policy of the government is that of competition.
I take it he meant competition in the field of transportation generally as well as in the field of aviation. The minister will remember that it is this policy of competition in the field of aviation which is causing the industry such concern. I am sorry that the Minister of Trans-[DOT]port is not in his seat at the moment because this is a matter which concerns him and more particularly his predecessor, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is responsible for much of the chaos in the field of aviation.
When the members of the government were on this side of the house they seized every opportunity at their command to demand competition and when they got into office they certainly went further than they intended to go with respect to competition in the field of aviation. The first thing the government did was to ask a British expert, Mr. Wheatcroft, to make a report on air line competition in Canada. I hold his report in my hand and I would point out that in this excellent report Mr. Wheatcroft recommended against competition in certain fields. Notwithstanding that fact, the government decided to grant a transcontinental air service to Canadian Pacific Airlines. According to many experts in the field, that policy and other policies of the government which I will deal with in a moment are responsible for the item which we have before us today to provide $6J million for the deficit of Trans-Canada Air Lines. In addition, Canadian Pacific Airlines had an equally high deficit in 1961 amounting to approximately $4 million.
The policy of the government has never been announced in the house for some reason or other, except piecemeal through an answer to a question or by a statement made by a minister outside the house, and to my mind this is very strange conduct on the part of the government. However, just prior to the election of 1958 the former minister of transport made a statement on aviation in which he said:
It is not intended to place T.C.A. or other Canadian air lines in competition with each other in the international field. International routes are set up by reciprocal agreement with other foreign countries, and provide rights for foreign air lines to operate over the same or equivalent routes. Therefore, plenty of competition already exists in the international field without the duplication which would result if Canadian air lines were made directly competitive over the same international routes.

That statement by the former minister of transport is quite clear, that there should be no competition between C.P.A. and T.C.A. on the international routes. But what did the government do? In the latter part of 1961 the government authorized Canadian Pacific Airlines to operate a route from Vancouver-Ed-monton to London. This was not only in contradiction of Canada's own policy in the field of international aviation but also in contradiction of the bilateral air agreement between Canada and the United States. Although Canadian Pacific Airlines announced in October of 1961 that it was going to start the new service from Vancouver-Edmonton to London and advertised the fact that these flights to London would originate in Vancouver and Edmonton, the company has not yet obtained permission so to do.
I have put many questions to the present Minister of Transport but he has evaded them continually and repeatedly by stating that conversations are going on between Mr. Peter Thorneycroft, minister of aviation of the United Kingdom, and the minister's officials. To those of us who sit on this side of the house it seems strange, having regard to the fact that it was first stated by the government that there would be effective competition and then later that there would be no competition in the field of international aviation, that the government, having announced a competitive international route, is not able to obtain permission for C.P.A. to land in London.
When told in the house that the government was out to destroy Trans-Canada Air Lines, as I stated, the present minister replied that competition on this route would be negligible and would not affect the government owned air line.
That is not what the minister said in a speech at Vancouver on December 4, 1961. At that time he stated that because of competition in world aviation the best interests of T.C.A. and C.P.A. would not be served in competing with each other and that there should be cooperation between the two. So we have this anomalous position. First, according to the former minister of transport, there should be no competition between T.C.A. and C.P.A. in international fields. Next, the present Minister of Transport announced in the house a new service for C.P.A. in the international field on the run Vancouver-Edmonton-London. Then the present minister stated in the house that this would not in any way affect T.C.A. and that the competition would be negligible. Three months later competition on international routes has suddenly become serious and there should be greater co-operation between C.P.A. and T.C.A.
The question arises in the minds of those who are interested in the field of aviation, 26207-1-188J

what is the policy of the government? Need I talk about the decontrol of class B aircraft announced by the former minister of transport which has caused such chaos among the small operators to the extent that there have been a large number of bankruptcies. Now it is being stated that it is the intention of the government, so the industry has been advised, to drop decontrol and put the situation back where it was before.
I think the government should make up its mind what its policy is going to be in the field of civil aviation. Is there going to be competition in the domestic services, is there going to be competition in the international services, or is the field going to be divided?
I think the government should inform the members of the industry, who I know are totally and wholly dissatisfied with the manner in which the government has outlined its policy from time to time.
I just want to say one further word because I do not want to hold up these estimates unduly. It has to do with Quebecair. Last year and the year before Quebecair was in very difficult circumstances and asked for assistance. The Minister of Transport stated that the air transport board would consider the position. The board did so and made several recommendations to the government. I understand that five recommendations were made including (a) a subsidy, (b) an operations payment during the winter and (c) a joint winter operations payment and a subsidy, but that treasury board on each and every occasion turned them down.
I know, of course, that the Minister of Finance will deny this but it is common knowledge in Rimouski that the person who held up this matter was none other than the Minister of Finance himself. It was common knowledge when I was down there not so long ago that, notwithstanding the recommendations of the air transport board and the desire of his colleague, the Minister of Transport, that a subsidy should be granted, the Minister of Finance was the one who held it up and decided against it. The minister will be free to deny that statement if he wishes to do so.
Then there is the other point, that the Minister of Transport told Quebecair in unequivocal and clear language that the government had decided to give that corporation exclusive air routes on the north shore of the St. Lawrence and, by inference, to take them away from T.C.A. Of that there can be no doubt. The Minister of Transport went a step further and said that such an announcement would be made by the government at a future time. There is no doubt about that; that is known all over the trade and in Quebecair offices. It is known in the air transport and

industries association and it is known in Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is known from one end of the industry to the other that that statement was made.
What happened was that the Prime Minister asked that the matter be held over- this was in the press-until such time as he returned from his trip to Japan. The Prime Minister returned from Japan, but nothing was done, other than, I take it, the Minister of Transport was slapped down because Quebecair is still waiting for its assistance. I need not tell the Minister of Finance that Quebecair needs the assistance. Quebecair is now under new management, and has had a total reorganization of its capital structure. There are new people at the head of the corporation. I am sure that they can do an excellent job. 1 ask the minister to give serious consideration to the recommendations that I know have been made, (a) by the Minister of Transport to the government and (b) by the air transport board to the minister.
One other thing I should like to mention and it is this. Quebecair asked the government to assist it in taking over one of the larger aircraft it had purchased from Cana-dair. This aircraft had been purchased at great cost. It was impossible at the time, several months ago, for Quebecair to use this aircraft profitably. I am informed that, notwithstanding the representations of Quebecair to the government to assist them in taking over that plane, either by representations to Canadair-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member at once that he is away out on his facts all the way through his speech. Let me begin with what he had to say about the deficit of Trans-Canada Air Lines. He has ascribed this to some aspect of competition and he complained about competition. Well, I would think the best authority on the reason for the Trans-Canada Air Lines deficit in the year 1961 would be the president of T.C.A. Here is what he said in his report, in explaining the deficit for 1961:
This was a paradoxical period of air line operations in which record traffic volume was accompanied by the largest deficit in the company's history. A new domestic fare structure proved immensely popular and there was a heavy increase in passenger business. Simultaneously, however, passenger demand shifted so emphatically towards economy class service that there was a pronounced deteriorating effect on the company's average revenue realized per passenger mile, this declining from 6,25 cents in 1960 to 5.81 cents in 1961. While 44 per cent of the company's passenger traffic had been economy class in the previous year, and an increase to 69 per cent had been forecast, the actual figure rose to 79 per cent. This revolution in travelling habits more than offset the company's achievement of substantial economies as evidenced by a very satisfactory reduction in operating cost per available ton mile from 36.72 cents to 31.30 cents. Obviously, this discrepancy between revenues and expenses requires remedial action.
This year's deficit amounted to $6,450,082.
Then the president goes on in his report to speak about the acquisition of new equipment, the cost of which of course is rising aU the time. So, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member, in what he had to say about the reason for this deficit is completely at odds with the president of the T.C.A. himself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I much prefer the reasoning advanced by the president of T.C.A.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Is the minister aware of the proceedings of the sessional committee on airlines and shipping, owned and operated by the government, at which evidence was given last year concerning the deficit of Trans-Canada Air Lines, in that competition was in large measure the answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The committee has not sat during this session. I am giving the statement of the president of T.C.A. because he outlined in his report the reason for this record deficit in the operations of the company in 1961. It should not be thought, Mr. Chairman, that this was the only time that Trans-Canada Air Lines had a deficit. It had deficits, smaller of course, in 1937, 1938, 1939, 1946, 1947, 1948, 1949, 1950 and 1960. These deficits could hardly be ascribed to competition, so I think the hon. member is quite wrong in his conclusions on this subject.
Now, he goes on to use this item to discuss a question with regard to the licensing operations of the air transport board. This discussion, Mr. Chairman, is quite irrelevant to the subject with which we are dealing here, the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines. Trans-Canada Air Lines is not the air transport board. The air transport board is given jurisdiction by this parliament in respect of licensing of air carriers. I suggest, therefore, that the subject be properly deferred to an occasion when it will be in order.
Now, the hon. member makes a strong plea for Quebecair. He has made what I think was about as strong a case of special pleading for a particular, privately owned company as I have ever heard in this house.

Factual gossip.

Mr. Chairman, I will only be a couple of minutes. I am not at all interested in gossip or rumours of any kind. However, I would like to ask the minister this question. Having regard to the five years the present government has been in office, what is his policy approach to crown corporations such as Trans-Canada Air Lines when they are initiated in the public interest and have done a terriffic job on behalf of Canada?
I can only say from my own point of view that after following five years of this government's policies and operations it does appear to me that their general policy is, if it affects a crown corporation, crash or smash, because only in the five years this government has been in office have we even heard talk of hurting crown corporations and turning them over to private enterprise by sale or competition, whether it be Eldorado, Polymer, or instituting measures that hit very hard at initiating services such as the C.B.C. and now T.C.A.
This matter can be discussed under this item. I think we have to honour the initiation of T.C.A., the pioneering it did, the service which it rendered. When it comes to a major transportation policy and difficulties arise, this government, instead of assisting, brings in completely unnecessary competition against a crown corporation which did the pioneering and was financed by the people. When it reaches a stage of major development, the government exercises a competitive policy.
I will not go any further than that, sir. I would like to ask the minister whether he can give us just a straightforward statement as to government policy with regard to crown corporations such as T.C.A.; whether

it is crash or smash, and why bring in competition at the expense of the Canadian people?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
Trans-Canada Air Lines has received at the hands of this government the fairest and indeed most generous consideration. The company has been provided with what it required to keep itself equipped with aeroplanes of the latest design and manufacture; indeed, enormous sums have been provided and expended in the equipment of the company for all its operations.
The action of the air transport board in the licensing of Canadian Pacific Airlines for a transcontinental flight daily to connect with overseas operations I presume, was based on the board's view that the time had come when Trans-Canada Air Lines was so fully established and so strong that it could face a measure of modest competition. But on this subject I really see no profit in getting into some doctrinaire discussion. The hon. member, according to his views, favours state monopoly in these matters. Some of the other hon. members of this chamber take a different view. I think we are not likely to harmonize those views this afternoon on this supplementary estimate.

Mr. Chairman, I think I must rise after the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, because in the province of British Columbia we have Canadian Pacific Airlines employing about 2,500 people; in fact, it provides one of the largest payrolls in the province of British Columbia. As a matter of fact it increased after the opening of the seaway; so if there has been an increase in employment in that area it is not due (a) to a diminution of the number of employees in the Department of Transport or (b) the St. Lawrence seaway authority, or (c) to the fact that the canal is on the other side [The Chairman.]
of the line. It is certainly not due to the fact that those employees on the canal ceased to work, because there were a small number employed there compared with the 4,258 people who are now out of employment.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows that every effort made by this government to assist the textile industry in providing tariff assistance was consistently, persistently and bitterly fought and opposed by the hon. member's own colleagues, and the most recent episode is that of the Senate turning down the class or kind legislation. The hon. gentleman also knows that the textile industry is now in a better condition than it has been for the past 20 years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In Cornwall?

No, not in Cornwall, because due to the neglect of the previous government the situation there was already too far gone to revive. In the same year that Cornwall Cottons declined Dominion Textiles made one of the highest profits it made for many years.
As far as the Cornwall seaway is concerned, the people of Cornwall know that it was locating the locks on the United States side that ruined Cornwall. Just ask the people of Cornwall about this. I suggest they will have an opportunity to give their answer very shortly and their answer will be found by the hon. member to be very pointed indeed. I would be delighted if the hon. gentleman were to come to Cornwall and oppose me in the constituency of Stormont. I would be delighted indeed if he were to do so.
He is afraid.
Of course he is.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Afraid of an oddball?

Does the hon. gentleman think that the Eisenhower and Snell locks on the United States side run themselves and that no one is employed on them? If they were located on the Canadian side in Cornwall they would certainly provide employment in that area.
I have several times contended-and I contend here and now-that the hon. member by his actions and by his neglect of the interests of this country and his former constituency-* his former home town-has made it impossible for there ever to be an all Canadian seaway in Canada. I say that for this reason. As we know the volume of traffic in the St. Lawrence seaway has been extremely disappointing but if for any reason it should ever increase perceptibly so that it becomes a threat to the New York port authority, you can be assured that all the vested interests centred in the New York port authority, the

financial and railway interests there, will insist that the Welland canal be bypassed by enlarging the Erie canal system so that not only will Cornwall be left high and dry as it now is-after Cornwall had been on the Cornwall canal for 120 years-but the whole St. Lawrence seaway including the port of Montreal will be bypassed by the new Erie canal. The new canal will bypass the Welland canal instead of twinning it, and traffic will be directed from the upper lakes and the interior of this continent down to New York with the result that the entire St. Lawrence system plus, to a degree, Halifax and Saint John will be bypassed.
Shame.

There was only one occasion on which we could have assured there being an all-Canadian seaway and that was at the time of the original construction when the hon. gentleman sold out to the United States. One of the most monumental blunders in the history of Canada was the error made by the hon. gentleman in relation to the failure to twin the Welland canal which was already reaching full capacity. It was as elementary a fallacy as to endeavour to increase the size of a bottle without increasing the neck.
These are the two fundamental errors the responsibility for which my predecessor, despite his canniness, evasiveness and agility with words has never been able to completely evade, and he has not convinced the people of Stormont. If he thinks he has, let me tell the hon. gentleman that the proof will be in the pudding and the opportunity to taste the pudding may come very shortly indeed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, one word in relation to what was said by the hon. member. Not a word was said by him in connection with the statements I have made, which are a complete answer-
I must examine those figures before commenting on them and learn the source of them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-which are a complete answer to the charges he has made in this house for the last five years.
May I point out that the hon. gentleman commenced his speech by saying he wished to ask me a question; but he forgot all about the question because he started ranting about everything under the sun. I simply wish to conclude my remarks by saying that no member from the constituency of Stormont since that constituency has existed has done more harm to his constituency than the present hon. member for Stormont.
Supply-Transport
Will the hon. member not agree that he sold out the interests of that constituency to the United States?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I say that for the following reasons, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman has said repeatedly that there are no pilots in the constituency when in fact there are at least 35 of them. He has said repeatedly there should be an amalgamation-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; what I said was that there were in the Cornwall area no native born pilots, no people born in Cornwall. There are pilots there who have simply moved in and located there overnight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. That is a question of debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has repeatedly said there should be an amalgamation of the C.N.R. and C.P.R. employees, thus putting out of work a large number of people in the Cornwall area which is a divisional centre of the C.N.R.
How many people are employed on the C.N.R. in Cornwall?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, on more than one occasion the hon. gentleman has said that a great deal of harm was constituted by the fact that Cornwall was not a seaway city. The other day the mayor of Cornwall celebrated the fact that Cornwall is now a seaway city. Notwithstanding the fact that the mayor of Cornwall and the industrial development corporation of Cornwall have repeatedly stated that Cornwall is a seaway city, the hon. member for Stormont insists that Cornwall is not on the seaway but is on high and dry land.
The hon. gentleman has emphatically stated and repeated that I am the one who is responsible for having effected the situation which exists today and he complains of there being no 27-foot facilities opposite Cornwall. The hon. gentleman does not know the facts. In point of fact, 27-foot facilities exist over a distance of three miles from Grace creek right up to the head of the locks at Cornwall. The hon. gentleman does not know that. As the member of parliament for the constituency of Stormont he should acquaint himself with at least the elementary situation obtaining in that area and cease to chase industry away; but no, notwithstanding the fact that the people of Cornwall are clamouring for industry to locate in that area the hon. member for Stormont insists on stating publicly that the seaway is on the other side of the line which in effect is tantamount to telling industry not to come to Cornwall because

Supply-Transport
there are no deep water facilities. Let me emphasize that the facilities are all there. If the hon. member for Stormont will only cooperate with the mayor of the city, the city council and the Cornwall industrial development corporation, industry will come to Cornwall.

Mr. Chairman, if there are facilities in Cornwall it is because of the fact that this government has spent over half a million dollars creating a port, which was done at the instigation of the present hon. member for Stormont. These 27-foot facilities now exist to intercept traffic before it goes south into the United States and to direct it back to Canada from the United States after proceeding through the Eisenhower and Snell locks. If there are facilities in Cornwall it is because of the efforts of the present hon. member for Stormont in persuading this government to attempt to retrieve some portion of the traffic we formerly had.
Furthermore, if my predecessor from this constituency produced so much benefit for Stormont, why did he abandon it, like a shepherd leaving his flock at the mercy of the wolves? The hon. gentleman abandoned that constituency. If he feels he did not abandon it I would be delighted if he were to return and oppose me in that constituency.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would certainly fix you if I ever came back.
Come back. I urge the hon. gentleman to come back. If the hon. member requires proof of my statements I urge him to take advantage of the opportunity of returning to that constituency as my opponent.
Mr. Chairman-
Carried.
If you want to get through you will have to let me ask one question.
A refugee from the seaway.
Carried.

I thank hon. gentlemen for the prompting. I wish to ask one question. Is the government aware that the United States corps of engineers has received a substantial grant from congress this year in order to carry out immediate study and planning for a United States canal that will save United States traffic going through the Welland canal? If so, what effect does the government think such a project, if proceeded with, will have on the prospects of the Welland canal and the adjacent area?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the government is well aware of that to which the hon. member has referred. The St. Lawrence seaway authority is embarking on studies in respect of the twinning of the locks but to endeavour to forecast at this time just what the outcome might be of any action such as has been suggested would, I think, be speculating more than I would like at this stage.

The point about which I wish to find out is whether the government is prepared to move very quickly if the United States engineers come up with a recommendation that would lead to a unilateral move on the part of the United States for a canal completely within the United States; that is to say one could foresee where this might take no notice of the St. Lawrence seaway authority at all. It is for that reason that I think we would all have considerable concern and would appreciate something a little bit more definitive about the position of the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. member is well aware of the rapidity with which the government is prepared to move at all times. However, in respect of this particular matter I should not like to speculate as to what the situation might be after some hypothetical action on the part of the United States government.

speechtext: Under this item I think it is in the national interest that we should come back to a matter of great importance, and one that has to do with a fundamental difference between an important official of the government of Canada and the government itself. It is a difference which, in principle, is not unlike the difference that arose and shook the foundations of government in Canada last summer in the dispute between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: They are as different as are day and night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I refer, of course, to the serious charge made by one of Canada's most distinguished sons. I refer to General McNaughton who said that the Columbia river treaty represented a sell out on the part of those who negotiated that treaty for Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Does the hon. member believe that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is not the
question. Whether I believe it or not is not the question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What I am saying is that a distinguished Canadian who has spent the greatest part of his life in the public service of this country has said that Canada was sold out by those who negotiated that treaty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
does not believe this, why does he repeat it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

That charge having been made, it should have come to parliament through the proper procedure for assessment as to validity. General McNaugh-ton asked that his charge be aired before a parliamentary committee of this House of Commons where we would have had an opportunity of examining him as to the nature of the indictment and where we would have had at the same time an opportunity of hearing from the ministers responsible, and the officials in order to determine the validity of this charge. Notwithstanding the requests made by the Leader of the Opposition and by other hon. members in this house, including the hon. member for Kootenay West, this government has delayed the opportunity of our discussing this matter in the way in which the matter is now about to be discussed.
This is not, of course, a new procedure for this government. It will be recalled that for many months we sought to bring before a committee of the House of Commons the former governor of the Bank of Canada so that that unfortunate dispute-bludgeoned by the action of the Minister of Finance- between that official and himself, could properly have been assessed by a committee of this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Notwithstanding the reluctance of the Minister of Finance to have the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada discussed by the banking and commerce committee and notwithstanding the reluctance of the government to allow the governor to come before that committee and discuss that report, we know that the governor was able to state his case in the other place before a committee of the non-elected members of this parliament.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

And a poor case it was.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
