speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not accurate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That dispute is now a matter of record. However, it will be recalled in the days and weeks to come. It will be discussed on the hustings, in the general elections about which we are soon to have an announcement. Let no one make any mistake about this. The people of Canada will indict this government for what they did and the manner in which they dealt with the Coyne affair. We now have a second Coyne affair which arises out of the charges made by General McNaughton.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Another Liberal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend says he is a Liberal. Surely that is not an offence in this country. Since when was it an offence? Let me tell my hon. friend that General McNaughton was a distinguished soldier in the first world war and was commander of the Canadian forces in the second world war. He was appointed to his first responsible office under the government of Canada when he was made chairman of the national research council by the government of which Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was prime minister. It was a Conservative appointment. He began his public service as an appointee of a Conservative government. From that time on he has rendered distinguished service to his country. No one can take that away from this distinguished Canadian. He has asked that he be allowed to come before a committee of this House of Commons so that he can make these serious charges. The Minister of Finance is not in his seat at the moment. This important matter is apparently being conducted now by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, although the Secretary of State for External Affairs apparently is now here holding a watching brief, whatever that may or may not be. The fact is that General McNaughton has made a serious charge. That charge should be heard. As he is not a member of this house, he
2960	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs cannot speak in this House of Commons. Consequently, he should be afforded the opportunity of going before a parliamentary committee.
If there was ever any doubt about the justifications for his request to have this matter placed before a parliamentary committee, we now have in justification a statement made by no less a person than the Minister of Justice who, according to a Canadian Press dispatch in this morning's paper is quoted as having said the following at Hanna, Alberta. I quote from a report of the Canadian Press which appears in this morning's Montreal Gazette, page 4.
Canada would have been better oft with a Columbia river treaty drawn according to General A. G. L. McNaughton's wishes, Justice Minister Davie Fulton said here.
Mr. Fulton said in an interview that it was not possible to draw the treaty in the manner Gen. McNaughton desired without treading on British Columbia's toes.
If General McNaughton had said nothing, this statement of the Minister of Justice would have been ample justification for our discussing this important matter. But coming on the heel of, or right after, or within a few days of the indictment levelled against this government by General McNaughton, this statement of the Minister of Justice now offers strong supporting justification for our request that a committee, namely the committee on external affairs, be set up forthwith

tonight, if necessary-so that there may be no delay in the government's plans with regard to dissolution. We can sit all day tomorrow; we can sit all night tonight, and determine whether or not there is validity in the indictment made against this treaty and against this government by General McNaughton. If the government refuses the request I am making today in support of that made by General McNaughton, then let the government stand in proper perspective in relation to the bill of rights about which the Minister of Finance spoke so vigorously two or three hours ago in this house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: And so eloquently.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
General McNaughton has made a charge. Under our bill of rights he should be given the opportunity of presenting his case before the highest court in the land, this parliament, through one of its committees. To deny General McNaughton that right on the eve of the dissolution of parliament will be an admission by this government that the charges made by General McNaughton and now supported by the Minister of Justice are justified.
The issue before us now is a simple one. It is not the merits of the treaty. It is the right of one who was in a position to know.


It is a question of examining the charges he has made with regard to the way in which the treaty was negotiated, a treaty which he says is not only contrary to our interests but with regard to which he says the Canadian people have been sold out by the government. In the face of these charges, serious charges supported by the Minister of Justice, this government will stand in contempt of parliament, in contempt of the Canadian people, if it denies the request I am making, that the external affairs committee be set up now. Set it up at six o'clock and we will sit throughout the hours to determine the validity of the serious charges made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on behalf of this party to support the request made by the hon. member for Essex East. I think he outlined very eloquently and properly General McNaughton's services to this nation, his contributions and his stature. He indicated that General McNaughton's first interest is to protect the interests of Canadian people and not go along with people in the United States because it is easier on occasions.
As far as the Columbia is concerned, Canada has come off second best for the second time in Canadian history. In 1846 the government of Great Britain signed the Oregon treaty and in return for the surrender of the land south of the 49th parallel and west of the Columbia river British subjects were guaranteed free access and navigation to the sea along the Columbia river in perpetuity under article 2 of the treaty. Many years later that treaty was followed by the building of dams by the United States government on the Columbia river. I do not blame the United States government but there was not a single protest from any agency of this government. I have had the record checked and not even the water resources branch was sufficiently alert to the position to warn the government that this was happening.
The former secretary of state for external affairs and present Leader of the Opposition had the records of the government searched at that time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That was under the former government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am trying to be quite fair. That is quite right; it was under the former government. I think it was a great omission that Canada's interests were not protected because I have talked to officials of various United States agencies who were amazed that we permitted these dams to be built without any protest in view of the impediment to navigation, the fact that there was no longer

access to the sea from the upper Columbia, the damage to our fishing interests and so on.
Now we come to this second occasion, the Columbia river treaty. General McNaughton has rendered great service to Canada and I am not going to repeat the many things that were said by the hon. member for Essex East. I was very disappointed, as I think many members of the house were, by the treatment of this gentleman who has given such great service to Canada in the first and second world wars. In fact, he was serving Canada before some of the advisers were bom. The announcement of his retirement was through a short and, I thought, very inadequate press release. I must bring it to the attention of the committee that a goodly number of lesser lights have had their retirements mentioned by way of announcement in this house. Personally I thought this was a rather shabby procedure on the retirement of a person who had rendered such great service to Canada. Mind you, that is not the attitude of the Canadian people or the Canadian press. I am already in receipt of sufficient telegrams and correspondence to realize what large sections of the Canadian people think of General McNaughton. However, to clinch that and to save time I am simply going to quote an editorial that appeared in the Vancouver Sun of December 18, 1959 under the heading "All Honour to Andy". It reads as follows:
General Andrew McNaughton has the stuff that makes great Canadians. He deserves official recognition for his outstanding victory in getting Canada a fair share of Columbia river downstream benefits. This feat will stand as a great achievement in the history of Canadian international bargaining. And as a landmark in Canadian economic development. It sets a precedent for future Canada-U.S. water control issues.
General McNaughton endured much uninformed and unfair political criticism on both sides of the border. But he knew his objective. He ignored all the irrelevancies. He developed a long-headed strategy. He stuck to it, to Canada's lasting benefit.
It is true he started from a position of strength. But he succeeded in making the other side recognize reasonably quickly that it had lost the battle. That avoided needless economic bloodshed by averting prolonged delay in coming to terms.
The five year climactic struggle began from what McNaughton described as a U.S. position of contending "with all the forces at its disposal" that Canada wasn't entitled to anything from the U.S. for controlling the Columbia. McNaughton was privately determined Canada would get 50 per cent of all the U.S. power gained. And get it in value holding electricity, not inflation vulnerable dollars.
His masterstroke was to refuse to truckle in any way to U.S. arrogance.
That is a very different attitude to some people I could mention.
He proposed diverting extra Columbia waters into the all-Canadian Fraser, thus depriving the U.S. of all benefits from Canadian control. He had international precedent. But the Americans thought he was bluffing. Then he ordered engineering
Supply-Northern Affairs studies of this gargantuan scheme. That might have been a big bluff. But the U.S. either overlooked it or couldn't nerve itself to call it.
Forces which preserve the Fraser for salmon could have blocked McNaughton's hydro scheme just as they've blocked all other hydro prospects there. A threat from late 1957 that Wenner-Gren development of the Peace river might jeopardize developing of the Canadian Columbia probably helped the Americans to see things General McNaughton's way sooner than they might have. But it can't account for the bonus he won in the settlement. Not only does Canada get 50 per cent of extra U.S. power, but the percentage is calculated on the gross increase, not the smaller net. And in 35 to 50 years Canada can still divert Columbia waters into the Fraser if that still makes hydroelectric sense.
I read that editorial because I think it outlines clearly what Canada owes to General McNaughton in one vast achievement which as a result of his tenacity and determination can mean in any future settlement millions of dollars in power value annually to Canadians for years to come.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Essex East that there have been so many contradictory statements made by persons of prominence on both sides of this issue and by both the federal and provincial governments that this gives greater reason for General McNaughton having the opportunity to be heard. General McNaughton has remained in office as a public servant since the treaty was signed. Because he was a public servant his lips were sealed. He was waiting week after week to have the opportunity to present his case before the external affairs committee, and I am quite sure he would soon knock the arguments of the water resources branch into a cocked hat. He waited week after week but without the opportunity being afforded.
Now he has the right to speak because he is no longer a public servant. General McNaughton does not bring this issue forward because of any interest in partisan politics. He takes this stand because of his strong conviction that Canada has received a poor deal in the Columbia river treaty. I recognize the fact that this treaty was, shall I say, forced or the terms of it were dictated to meet the wishes of the provincial government. But the situation is such that it never can be clarified in the minds of Canadians unless we have General McNaughton before the external affairs committee. The members of this party agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Essex East, that we will sit here tonight and tomorrow or as long as is required to complete this business.
Then, in addition to that, the government has promised all the chambers of commerce, farmers institutes and other organizations in the Kootenays, the Arrow lakes, the water resources committees, that they will be advised when this committee is to sit and given an

Supply-Northern Affairs opportunity to present their case. We will even continue in session long enough for them to get to Ottawa and present their case in connection with certain aspects of this treaty.
I mentioned that there were a great many contradictions, and I want to deal with them briefly. When the Prime Minister signed the treaty he made a few brief remarks, and I quote one paragraph:
In conclusion, the treaty that is being signed today is without precedent in the relations between nations. It represents a new level of co-operation for mutual advantage. Without the proposed agreement neither country could secure benefits for its people equal to those that can be realized through the action that the treaty contemplates.
Now, that is what the Prime Minister said on that occasion. Then, what did the Minister of Justice say in an address to the Canadian club in Montreal on February 13, 1961? He said:
I would like to stress at this point that the government of British Columbia was closely associated with these negotiations and gave wholehearted approval to the plans unfolded in the treaty negotiations.
I am quite confident that is an accurate statement on the part of the Minister of Justice. What does Mr. Bennett say when he refuses to go along with the terms of this treaty? A recent statement made by the Minister of Justice indicates that the federal government bowed to the wishes of the province of British Columbia. What does Mr. Bennett have to say? I have a copy of his address made at Prince George on September 16, 1961. He was kind enough to send me this copy from his office. I quote:
Well, as you know, the United States and Canada have signed a treaty. It has been ratified by the congress of the United States but not by the parliament of Canada. As you know, too, British Columbia has agreed to the general engineering principles outlined, but has never agreed to the financial proposals put forth by the government of Canada.
The reason we have not agreed to those proposals is very simple: We want at-site power on our Columbia river installation as soon as possible. And to bring that about, we must dispose of our surplus power at a fair and equitable price.
It might be asked, "Well, what of it? Look at now much you're getting and how little you're giving away".
All right-let's look. But let's not even look through my eyes, because after all, I may be prejudiced. Let's look instead through the eyes of the secretary of the interior of the United States of America, Mr. Stewart L. Udall.
Mr. Udall is the member of President Kennedy's cabinet who has the direct responsibility of seeing that the Columbia river treaty is carried out by the United States. Recently, he issued a statement on the treaty. I have a copy of the statement with me tonight, and because it is so extremely important that we understand clearly what the treaty implies, I am going to quote rather fully from his remarks.
In any event, Mr. Udall goes on to discuss the effect of the Canadian storage at the

Arrow lakes, Duncan and Mica creek. Then, he says:
As each of the Canadian storages become operable, the resulting improvement in flows can be utilized by generators already installed in the existing U.S. projects. Most of the U.S. projects were originally constructed with additional generators for reasons of economy of construction, anticipation of load growth and the subsequent availability of additional storage.
Then, Mr. Bennett said:
I quote again from Mr. Udall's statement: "To provide flood control and power benefits equivalent to those provided by the Canadian storage as of 1970 entirely from projects in the United States would require an investment in the United States of about $710 million over the next nine years. To realize these benefits through Canadian storage, on the other hand, the costs in the United States over that period are estimated at not over $150 million."
That is point No. 3, and it needs no further comment from me. Here is point No. 4:
"Because of the relatively small new incremental investment required on our part, Canadian storage yields power quickly and at an extremely low cost to the United States. The delivered cost... is less than one half the present basic wholesale power rate of the Bonneville power administration."
Again, no further comment is needed from me.
There is a great deal more in Mr. Udall's statement, and I would be glad to have you look at it. But for the sake of illustrating what we give and what we get from the treaty, I believe the examples I have quoted will suffice.
And so here, to summarize, is what we are giving:
Canada will provide one natural resource, our water, and surrender another, our land which will be flooded forever.
Canada must finance, pay for, engineer, construct and maintain forever all the storage dams.
By carrying out the development, Canada will give the United States 50 per cent more storage- which means the power of another Grand Coulee dam, plus flood control, plus irrigation benefits, plus navigation control-all at a fraction of the amount it would cost the United States to realize these benefits if it were to carry out the work on its own side of the boundary.
And over and above all this, the Columbia treaty gives the United States the right to build the Libby dam in Montana, a dam which they have wanted to build for many years, and one which will yield them great benefits.
That is the "little bit" which Canada is giving under terms of this treaty.
And what are we getting?
Sixty four million dollars in compensation for our flooded land, plus half of the so-called "downstream benefits".
This is the package the government of Canada has been pressing British Columbia to accept. This is the deal which the zealous-and in my opinion, extremely naive-chief Canadian negotiator, the Honourable E. Davie Fulton, wants British Columbia to buy.
We say this is not good enough, either for British Columbia, which has the most to lose, or for Canada. We agree that the treaty can be made to work, but only if the potential benefits to Canada are brought back into balance with the certain sacrifices of Canada.
Then, after Mr. Bennett makes that statement, we had the minister of lands and forests in British Columbia saying what a wonderful

treaty this is. Can you understand the confusion in the minds of the public when we have these various statements? Then, we have the Minister of Justice speaking to the Prince George chamber of commerce, when he outlined very clearly that this treaty was signed with the United States and he criticized Mr. Bennett very strongly for his statement. I quote:
The Bennett juggernaut even tried to roll over the treaty itself-to discredit the terms Bennett's own minister, the Honourable Ray Williston had worked out with us during a year of hard work and splendid co-operation. You are told we are trying to ram this treaty down the throats of an unwilling British Columbia. What a monstrous proposition. The B.C. government helped make the treaty. The B.C. government endorsed the treaty. The B.C. government is primarily responsible for many of its most important terms. Why the abrupt change about the treaty? Why did the Bennett government cast out its own creation?
Then, later on we had this statement from the Minister of Justice, to which reference has already been made, to the effect that Canada would have been better off with a Columbia treaty drawn according to General McNaughton. In view of these contradictory statements, and in view of the great confusion in the public mind, we wholeheartedly support the proposal for bringing General McNaughton immediately before the external affairs committee.
With regard to this treaty I think the federal government received very poor advice from its water resources branch. The officials of this branch just look at things in terms of power and kilowatts; they do not look at things in terms of land, natural resources and values of that sort. The treaty was signed by this government with no definite knowledge of where the site would be for the High Arrow or Duncan dams. Premier Bennett has said the provincial government has spent $500,000 a month for the last eight months in order to determine whether they could build dams on these sites. The locations of the dams have been decided without any regard to the land to be flooded, the damage to agriculture, to the forest industry or the detriment that will be caused to the fishing resources. The damage caused will cost millions of dollars to restore, according to the wildlife service of British Columbia. This government has not considered the compensation that will be required because of the destruction of beaches, wharves, roads and ferries.
In addition to that, until recently the water resources branch did not know anything about the cost of moving logs from one side of the dam to the other. I have been told by prominent engineers attached to a large corporation that it will cost $25 million to build the equipment to lift nearly one million feet of logs a day over the High Arrow dam.
Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is nonsense.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance says, "Nonsense". Does the parliamentary secretary think he has better knowledge than at least three top-notch engineers in Canada who were employed by this company and spent weeks studying this question? They have said it will cost $25 million to install the equipment to move the logs over this dam automatically. That is not provided for in the estimates of cost at all. Or, I am informed, the government will have to pay this company $500,000 a year in perpetuity, if equipment costing two or three million dollars is installed.
I am not blaming the federal government for this; I think they were very poorly advised by some of their own officials. How can you say that a treaty is a satisfactory one if you do not know what your costs will be, and other engineering firms have indicated that the cost of these dams is underestimated by over $100 million. I am not blaming the government for these figures, but I do say that the situation is such that General McNaughton, with his known capacity in this field and with his knowledge and experience from which the house and the public can be properly informed on this situation, should be called before the external affairs committee to tell his story. I am sure when that story is told he will convince his most caustic critics that he is the man who has the answers.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this problem is a very good example of people, with the best intentions, getting into a great deal of difficulty. I happen to be a native of the Columbia watershed; in fact, I was born about the centre of that portion of the Columbia watershed which is in Canada. My people were pioneers in that whole district. One was a member of parliament for Kootenay and then for many years a senator for Kootenay; so I have been particularly close to this picture from the time it first came before the standing committee on external affairs, which must be ten years ago. I can assure hon. members that I have never had the slightest intention of allowing that portion of my native province to be subjected to any deal which was unfair, and that is still my intention today.
I am afraid the hon. member for Essex East has overlooked the answer I gave to a question asked by him on April 9 which will be found at page 2641 of Hansard. He asked that General McNaughton be allowed to appear before the external affairs committee and my answer, speaking for the government, was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has already given the assurance that before the treaty is ratified

Supply-Northern Affairs
it will be referred to the standing committee on external affairs, and at that time I would hope that General McNaughton could be called and give whatever evidence he wishes.
The treaty has not yet been ratified. There is no intention of ratifying it without putting it before the standing committee on external affairs. Personally I would be delighted to see General McNaughton, the residents in my old home district and anybody else appear before that committee, because the one thing in which I am interested is seeing that the treaty is a proper one and that the Columbia is developed in the best interests of the Canadian people.
Let us not hear any more of this idea that the government is trying to rush this thing through without giving General McNaughton a chance to appear, because that is not the case at all. Hon. members have had the assurance of the government that before this treaty is ratified it will be submitted to the standing committee on external affairs.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Can we rely on that assurance?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is not the
point; it may never be ratified.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I know that the hon. member for Laurier, who is a very old friend of mine, would not wish to intimate that my word is not good.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman; could I tell the minister at once that that would be the last thing in my mind. But I was thinking of the business of the house and assurances that we have received that certain business would be brought forward, and it never was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not right; that is absolutely incorrect.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would be very doubtful that this matter could be dealt with before Easter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is one other point, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are too honest to be a politician.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Some comment has been made about the statement reported to have been made in Alberta by the Minister of Justice yesterday or the day before. Like myself, the Minister of Justice is a native of British Columbia and his people have a longer record than my own in the public life of that province; they have a very distinguished record. He has stated, which is the fact, that originally we negotiated with the United States on the basis of a dam being put in the east Kootenays on the Kootenay river.


There must be a dam go in on that river either in Canada or in the United States in order to stop the flooding. With the consent of the government of British Columbia and with their approval we got the Americans to agree that that dam could be put in east Kootenay in Canada. I think that was very much to the surprise of the government of British Columbia. But then they turned right around and changed their minds completely and said "We will not stand for a dam in east Kootenay", and the result was that the term of the agreement had to be that the dam would be at Libby in Montana.
General McNaughton wanted the dam in Canada; so did the Canadian negotiators. The Minister of Justice quite properly stated that in his speech which is reported in the papers this morning. He is not to be condemned for that. The fact is that all through the conference General McNaughton was kept right in the picture, and kept in by me because he came under me as the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I wanted him in there to see that everything was as it should be. When it came to the final question as to whether the treaty should be recommended, the general did not like some of the features of it; he said, "I cannot oppose it. I cannot recommend it, but I cannot oppose it".
That was his position a week or so before the treaty was signed. Now, apparently, he is a great deal more antagonistic toward the treaty. In the intervening months I think he has been filled by the conviction that the treaty is very much worse than it appeared to him to be at that time. I do not want to be critical of General McNaughton but I can only repeat the leading paragraph on an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 11-and everybody knows that the Winnipeg Free Press is one of the strongest supporters of the Liberal party in Canada. It says:
General McNaughton's attack on the Columbia river treaty, which he helped to negotiate, comes very late. If he believed that the treaty was a bad bargain he should have opposed it before it was signed by the Canadian government, when a better version might have been arranged.
Indeed, if he felt, as he now says, that the treaty "sold Canada down the river," he should have resigned as Canadian chairman of the international joint commission, a step which would certainly have made any government hesitate to approve the scheme. Instead, according to the government, he accepted the treaty as the best obtainable, though it was known that he had urged a somewhat different engineering design. Now, when he is being retired from his office, he suddenly tries to lock the bam door while the horse is a long way down the road.
I am pleased today that there is not the same emphasis on General McNaughton having been dismissed, or having been removed, as we heard in this chamber on

Monday. I do not want to go over the discussion which took place at that time but I would point out again that General Mc-Naughton has been under my jurisdiction. He was not dismissed; he was not removed. His retirement came just by reason of years-he had reached the age of 75 years. There was Mr. Dansereau, who had long service on the international joint commission, reaching that same age last year and he was not reappointed. It was simply and solely because of age that General McNaughton was not appointed again. He had been appointed on a year to year basis by the former government when the present Leader of the Opposition was Secretary of State for External Affairs and there was not the slightest idea of taking any action against General McNaughton because of the Columbia river problem or because of any other problem. It was solely a matter of age.
Here again I have an editorial from another leading Liberal newspaper-in fact, these two papers are the two toughest Liberal papers in Canada-This one is the Toronto Star and it said on April 9:
As for his charge that he has been fired by a "dictator", the general has, in our view, no reasonable cause for complaint. The fact is that he has more than completed his 12-year term as Canadian chief on the international joint commission and the government chose not to renew his appointment.
They are incorrect in referring to a 12-year term because there is no such animal. The General was appointed each year. The article continues:
His statement that he is an international civil servant does not hold water. As a Canadian appointee, heading the Canadian section of the commission, he was responsible to the Canadian government. And the government was perfectly entitled to retire him if it wished.
I would suggest that further criticism along these lines would be unfair not only to the government but also to General McNaughton himself, because it is going to do something to injure his splendid reputation and I can only ask for that fact to be kept in mind. I repeat that before the treaty is ratified it will be possible for the standing committee on external affairs to consider this question, and whatever evidence is brought before it can be heard. Then we can perhaps all agree on a treaty which is in the best interests of Canada.
I must say in conclusion that I think a good deal of the criticism should be directed west, out to the Pacific, rather than here to Ottawa. We have certainly done the best we could for Canada. We have not done any changing of our minds or pulling out of rugs as has been done by some of the others involved in this complicated problem
Supply-Northern Affairs and I really do not think it is fair that very much of the blame should be directed to Ottawa.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister a question. I have just received notice from the press that Mr. Bennett called a press conference this morning and asked the Canadian government to ratify the Columbia treaty immediately.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not sure whether the hon. member is trying to get on the same side as Premier Bennett or not. He seems to be in an awful hurry to get the external affairs committee to meet. I do not know whether he wants to get the treaty ratified or not. But Premier Bennett is not running the Canadian government yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be permitted to say a few words in the light of what the minister has said on this matter. I am sorry I was not here to listen to my hon. friend from Essex East, but I understand he did not deal with the merits of the Columbia treaty itself. At this particular moment it is not the matter at issue, though it would lend itself to an interesting discussion if the opportunity should arise. I understand, also, that my hon. friend did not deal with the dismissal of General McNaughton as such but that he was asking for an investigation into the statements made by General McNaughton as a member of the Canadian section of the international joint commission-statements made by him regarding his dismissal and statements made regarding the nature of the treaty which we have mentioned. That is the issue as we have raised it at this time.
Surely, since the Coyne affair there has never been a matter which has cried more loudly for examination and investigation than this one does. The minister said that General McNaughton had not been dismissed, and he quoted some sources which were completely satisfactory to him on this matter. General McNaughton, he said, had not been dismissed; he had merely been allowed to retire at the end of the year's period of extension which had characterized for some years his position as chairman of the international joint commission. In other words, he was holding that office from year to year. That may be the attitude taken by the minister, but I should like to quote an authority which will be equally respectable in the eyes of the hon. gentleman-the Toronto Telegram, which everyone knows is very close to the government in this and other matters.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The government's conscience.

Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The Toronto Telegram, had this to say on Monday, April 9:
General McNaughton's blast against government policy on the Columbia river is typical of this embittered old man-
I must say that is a rather ungenerous comment concerning a man who has served Canada as General McNaughton has served, but we will let that pass. The editorial then goes on to say:
He has been fired from his job as chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission-
Then there was the statement made by General McNaughton himself. If, however, the situation is as the minister states it, then surely this is one reason-and it is only one reason and perhaps not the most important- why there should be a chance to reconcile the conflicting statements in regard to this question of his dismissal. That could be done very simply by asking General McNaughton to appear before the committee on external affairs of this house.
There are other statements made by General McNaughton which have also been contradicted by spokesmen of the government. Surely it is a matter of great interest and importance to have these contradictions resolved for the sake of everybody concerned, including the government.
On April 3 the Prime Minister announced the general's retirement. He announced it outside the house in a press statement in which he said that he wished to take the opportunity of expressing the government's appreciation of the distinguished service General McNaughton rendered to Canada over so long a period of time and in so many important fields, a tribute which I think most hon. members of this committee would echo.
It would be very interesting to know, and perhaps the minister will be able to tell us, the circumstances surrounding the issue of the statement of April 3. Was General McNaughton formally apprised of the fact that his position was not to be continued, that he was going to be dropped at the end of this year's extension, if I may use that expression?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I can clear that up at once, Mr. Chairman. I spoke to General McNaughton myself some weeks before this announcement. We had a perfectly amicable discussion and arrangement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On April 6, three days after the statement was made, which, according to the minister was the result of a very amicable arrangement made between him and the general-apparently the general did not consider it exactly in this light-the general


made a statement in Washington which has been given a good deal of publicity. In that statement he said he had been removed and he was quite emphatic as to what had happened.
As I said, that is perhaps the least important aspect of this unhappy episode. The general, having said that his retirement was due to an arbitrary decision-and he went on to say of a dictator-on the same day also expressed very serious reservations about the treaty. Perhaps he felt free to express those reservations only after he had been informed-or the country had been informed -by a press release from Ottawa that he was about to vacate his post. That being the case, General McNaughton might have felt free to say things he could not have said while occupying his position. I need not repeat what he said on that occasion about the treaty because it has already been placed on the record. On April 7, the next day, the Minister of Justice took issue, as I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs also did, with the statement made by the general in respect of this treaty, and whether or not it was in the best interests of Canada.
The general in his turn has taken issue with some of the statements made by representatives of the government. He said on April 7 that he informed the government at the time that he would not associate himself with the treaty and he made it clear to the full federal technical committee that he would speak his mind when the opportunity arose. The opportunity arose after the general was told his term of office was over. Surely this is the kind of thing that should be investigated by the committee on external affairs of this house. If ever there was an important issue to submit to this committee, such a vital subject, this is it. I should have thought the government would have been the first to desire that this matter be looked into by a committee of this house in that way.
Another reason for having such a committee meet at once arises from the statement made yesterday, and an explanation of which was offered today to the effect, according to the Canadian Press, that the plan submitted by General McNaughton at the time was a better one than that which was actually signed in relation to the Columbia, but that it was impossible and impracticable to bring it about at that time.
Another reason for investigating this matter arises from the statement issued by the general this afternoon and from the press conference held by the premier of British Columbia this morning. All these matters

have thrown this whole question into confusion and indeed into disarray. Surely the committee on external affairs, while parliament is sitting, is the place where some of this confusion we would hope could be removed and where we could be given the opportunity of finding out what actually has happened, not only in connection with General McNaugh-ton's charges against the government and the negotiation of this treaty but also in connection with the treaty itself. In this way we might have an opportunity before this parliament ends of looking into the treaty. I do not quarrel with anything the minister said with respect to the treaty being submitted to the committee on external affairs before ratification. That, of course, is the convention and the custom under our constitution, that parliamentary approval should be given to every international engagement or treaty which imposes any commitments or obligations on this government, this country or this parliament. That is the normal course of events. That is what happens. These matters do not always go first to the committee on external affairs, although it has been the practice to submit conventions and treaties first to that committee, and then they are referred back to the full House of Commons.
Ever since this treaty was signed-and it was signed in circumstances which made it very doubtful indeed whether ratification would be easy and early because of the attitude taken by the province of British Columbia in connection with it-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: After it was signed that attitude was taken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That attitude became pretty clear in the letter sent by the premier of British Columbia to the Minister of Finance on, I believe, January 13, 1961, only a day or so, I admit, before the signature.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In that respect may I point out that perhaps the Leader of the Opposition is unaware that ministers from British Columbia and their officials had been sitting in all the way through and had agreed to every word of the treaty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am indeed aware of that, Mr. Chairman. I am aware of the fact that representatives of British Columbia took part in the negotiations. I assure the minister that I am not disposed any more than he is to give any particular credit to the government of British Columbia for the way it has handled this matter. Nevertheless before the treaty was actually signed, and notwithstanding the fact that representatives of the government of British Columbia sat in on the negotiations, the premier of British Columbia sent a letter
Supply-Northern Affairs to the Minister of Finance in which he expressed very grave doubts about the implementation of this treaty, especially on the financial side.
It was not too late even then, in view of the doubts on the part of British Columbia as expressed by the premier, to have waited until those last minute doubts were removed. Surely this made it desirable that this treaty should go to some committee of the House of Commons at the earliest possible date, especially in the light of the difference that had arisen between the province of British Columbia and the federal government.
If those differences could not be resolved there was no possibility, as I see it, of the federal government carrying through its signature to ratification. It would be idle to ratify or give parliamentary approval to an international treaty if that treaty could not be implemented through the co-operation of the province which was essential to its implementation. This was surely the time when we should have had an opportunity to examine this treaty before the committee during those months.
Over the past months I have put a good many questions to the government in regard to this matter. On March 24, 1961 as reported at page 3304 of Hansard I asked the Prime Minister whether we could expect that this treaty would be submitted to this parliament shortly for consideration. In replying the Prime Minister said:
I wish to make it clear that it will be submitted but the date when it will be submitted still remains to be considered.
Then I said a little later on that, while recognizing the difficulties of discussing a treaty in a committee before these difficulties had been resolved with the province, nevertheless we hope these difficulties can be resolved without delay, at least to the point where we can examine this treaty in parliament.
The Minister of Justice said that he agreed that the proper place to do that was before the committee on external affairs, when there would be the fullest discussion and fullest vindication of the terms of this treaty.
An entirely new situation has now arisen. If that situation had not arisen, perhaps we would not be justified in requesting consideration before this committee of this treaty in the dying days of a parliamentary session. However, this is an entirely new situation now, when the chairman of the international joint commission who has so much to do with the negotiations of this treaty makes with regard to it certain statements which are, to say the least, important and which have been contradicted by the government itself. We still have some days
2968	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs in this parliament. No one knows how many. However, we have enough in which to ask tor the committee to be convened at once and to ask General McNaughton to appear before this committee and to tell this House of Commons what he means when he says that Canada was sold down the river when this treaty was signed. The government owes that consideration, in justice to itself as well as to parliament. While statements remain unchallenged, except by statements made on the other side by ministers, this is the time to resolve the differences. The ministers say one thing. General McNaughton says something else. Premier Bennett says something else out in British Columbia. The Minister of Justice says one thing in Ottawa and something else out in Alberta. If there was ever a time when a situation was confused and was dangerous in its confusion, and if there ever was a time when that kind of situation should be cleared up, surely this is it. Surely the minister will realize the advisability of calling this committee together at once, not for the reasons about which we have been talking in the past, namely to go into all the articles of the treaty, although that would be desirable, but to get this single problem solved: Who is right with regard to statements made about this treaty?

speechtext: This is another Coyne affair.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Two sides to the coin; two flags.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As a member of this House of Commons from British Columbia speaking on this most important issue now before us, may I say that I am not interested in saying anything about the retirement, whether forced or otherwise, of General McNaughton. I am interested in only one thing. I refer to a situation which, because of misunderstandings, charges and countercharges and a tirade of abuse between governments, has resulted in no action over the years in the development of hydro power resources in my province, with particular reference to development in the Columbia river basin.
I wish to say that in the years during which I have had the honour of being a representative of British Columbia I have never before known of a situation which was so heartbreaking as that relating to the power potentiality and development in British Columbia. I think there has been a great deal of misunderstanding. I think there has been far too much politicking, with the result that the general public do not know who is telling the truth and who is lying. A further result has been that development, which should have started a long time ago, is still to come, perhaps some time in the distant 

future. If the story were fully known, I believe it would make one of the most fantastic stories in the history of Canada. We have as the premier of British Columbia one who regards himself as a king maker, himself to be king with a British Columbia empire.
From my knowledge of British Columbia I feel absolutely safe in saying, without fear of any honest contradiction, that several years ago the government of British Columbia made some kind of backhand agreement with a corporate power in the United States for a certain development on the Columbia. From what I know, and as far as I can know, of that backhand arrangement, I have no hesitation in saying that had it not been for the action taken by the present government there might have been the greatest sellout ever known in Canada on the Columbia and its power potential. Because action was taken by this government to prevent that sellout, we then had a northern vision, not of this government but of the premier of British Columbia, wherein once again there was an agreement-the full details of which I maintain are not known and perhaps never will be known- as to the development of the power on the Peace river. Hence between politics, and the egotism, ambitions and desires of the premier of British Columbia we have had develop that extraordinary situation of a great deal of talk, charges, countercharges, abuse, and passing of the buck, and no development, be it on the Columbia river or on the Peace river.
We have in British Columbia this terrific potential power both in the south and in the north. Its development can be determined only by the two responsible governments getting together for the purpose of co-operating in the interests of British Columbia and of Canada. The matter is never going to be resolved by the continuation of what we have now and what we have had in the past between the two governments. Moreover, I feel quite safe in saying that the development of these two potentials, namely the Columbia and the Peace, cannot come to fulfilment without complete provincial and federal cooperation, as the hydro potential of the two put together is so great that it can be utilized only by a national power grid system if both are to proceed at the same time.
However, Mr. Chairman, our main and perhaps only concern at this moment is the Columbia river basin and its development by arrangement between the federal government and the government of the United States, and between the federal government and that of the province of British Columbia. I believe that the spirit of co-operation and compromise has been missing over the years. I believe that

two reasonable and sensible governments, although they have failed to get together in the past, owe it to the people of British Columbia and of Canada generally to resolve their difficulties and to do so very quickly; but they can only resolve their difficulties by complete honesty and a full statement of the facts.
I agree entirely with the statement of our house leader, the hon. member for Kootenay West, and the statement of the Leader of the Opposition, that the way to arrive at the facts and an understanding of the true situation so as to be able to pinpoint what is the best thing to do and how to proceed in the future is to have all those concerned, the federal government, the provincial government, the United States authorities and General McNaughton, appear before a committee of this house with that committee having absolute authority to call for persons and papers.
I think the government must accept a great deal of responsibility for the situation which has arisen. With their knowledge of the situation, I believe they should have been in a position to have the committee meet a long time ago and thereby clear the air. I believe that the government, perhaps unwittingly, though it is hard to say, has allowed itself to be made the stooge of the premier of British Columbia and has been made to play his game whereby as a result of the trading of abuse and the lack of action, he has been able to say that he cannot proceed because of the federal government.
This is the senior government and as such it has complete control of licensing on international rivers and waters. Having that in mind, the federal government should have been in a position to put Premier Bennett on the spot and make him put up or shut up, prove or disprove. I regret that a firm attitude of this sort has not been adopted by the federal government up till now.
I also want to say that I believe the statements made by General McNaughton are such that they cannot be ignored by the government. The government owes it to the people of Canada in general and the people of British Columbia in particular to make provision as speedily as possible so that General McNaughton, with his ten years of study and knowledge in this field, may be able to present his facts in perspective, and to give the reasons why he has made his recent charges, which I think have been confirmed by the recent statement of the Minister of Justice in Hanna, Alberta, as quoted by the hon. member for Kootenay West. If the newspaper report is correct this is something which the senior government cannot ignore. The minister has said that a Columbia river treaty drawn according to General A. G. L.
Supply-Northern Affairs McNaughton's wishes would have been better for Canada, but that it was not possible to draft a treaty in the manner suggested by General McNaughton without treading on British Columbia's toes. I say that under the British North America Act and having regard to the powers of the federal government one man should not be allowed to dictate something which is against the best interests of his own province and the people of Canada. I wish to emphasize that I believe it would not be in the interests of Canada and I know it would not be in the interests of British Columbia for the matter of the Columbia river basin development to be made a political issue in the federal election. This matter transcends politics. It transcends speeches on the hustings. It concerns the development of the hydro potential of British Columbia and is a matter which should be discussed and decided away from the field of politics by reasonable men and women, whether they be in the provincial legislature or the House of Commons. Although the time may now be very short before the dissolution of the 24th parliament of Canada, it is my sincere hope that some method will be found immediately to have this matter clarified and settled while we are still here.
I must conclude now but I want to repeat what I said in beginning my remarks. This is not a matter of the federal government saving face, of Premier Bennett and the Social Credit government of British Columbia saving face or of General McNaughton saving face. Development of the Columbia river is a matter of great importance and something that is essential to British Columbia. In all fairness I must say that it is also of importance to the states south of the British Columbia border.
I hope that viewpoint will be recognized and appreciated and that some way will be found by immediate negotiation with the province of British Columbia to bring this matter to a reasonable conclusion, so that a start can be made very soon on the development and so that we may bring to an end the trading of abuse and charge and countercharge. We have a greater responsibility than to deal with this matter in the way it has been dealt with up to now.

I am particularly interested in statements that have been made within the last day or two about the possibility of the resumption of nuclear tests and the possibility of postponing these tests as the result of some kind of


interim agreement. There is a report, and I am paraphrasing it, to the effect that the Canadian government-the minister referred to this this morning-made what were called representations to Washington; and that certain delegations to this conference from the so-called uncommitted countries have also made representations, to the effect that the United States should not resume tests even though there is no satisfactory or, indeed, any agreement about control or inspection. I wonder if the minister feels he could tell us something about the thinking of the government in connection with this matter? I ask this question, not in any controversial or critical sense, but because the matter is of such tremendous importance. If the minister could give any clarification of the position of the government, I think it would be helpful.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

A day or two ago, in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition, I read from my first speech in Geneva to indicate the stand we had taken at that time about the tests. Of course that is still the Canadian position and is very clearly understood by all the nations concerned. Attempts are still being made in the conference in Geneva to work out some agreement between the nuclear powers which will result in a test ban treaty. It is impossible to say whether or not these efforts will be successful.
While there may not be agreement reached on a treaty which would provide for no more tests, I think there is also an intermediate position which is that tests should be postponed in the hope that something can be worked out. We are doing the best we can, but at the moment I cannot give the house any assurance as to what the final result will be.

Well, the big controversy between the nuclear powers is as to the type of verification there must be. The Soviet union claims that all the verification necessary can be obtained by the national systems of the western countries. The United States and the United Kingdom maintain there must be some international verification in each of the nuclear countries. Now, the dividing line is not entirely clear. I think there is some scope in there for bargaining. The parties on each side may have been taking a more rigid position than they would adopt as a final position.
Scientific matters are also involved in the question of what can be verified. I think it has been generally agreed that they have been verifying explosions in the atmosphere. The whole dispute is about explosions underground. One of the questions is whether or not there would have to be posts in the Soviet union and the United States, international posts, or whether it would be sufficient to send in inspection teams after there had been seismic disturbances which had not been definitely identified. Now, I believe there is some scope in that field for the two sides to get together. In any event, that is Canada's hope.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a word on this question. It is a vital matter. I know the minister is concerned about it. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, our discussion on this matter is in no way political. All we are seeking to do is make a contribution toward the solution of one of the vital problems which faces mankind at the present time.
As I understand the situation, the government of the United States has said through its president that it must resume tests; that this resumption is necessary because of the inability of the United States and the Soviet union to agree on a program for the cessation of nuclear tests under conditions which the United States believes would not prejudice its security.
The Soviet union detonated some very major nuclear weapons last fall. The suggestion is that as a result of such explosions the Soviet union acquired information with regard to problems having to do with anti-missile operations. All I am now saying is what one reads in publications. Indeed, the leader of the Labour party in the United Kingdom has gone so far as to express the view that the Soviet union may have acquired information as a result of these latter explosions which, while not adding to the deterrent strength of the Soviet union, nevertheless gives that country some information in that particular field which may not be open at this time to the United States. It is suggested that this is one of the reasons why the President of the United States has decided to resume tests. The leader of the Labour party in England, Mr. Gaitskell, in a public speech in his country indicated that he would favour the resumption of tests because of these conditions and circumstances which are alleged to have followed the explosions by the Soviet union.
This is the background. I am assuming that notwithstanding this situation, the view of the government of Canada is that the United States should not resume tests, whether or not it is able to reach an agreement at Geneva with regard to the resumption of such tests. I understand further that the

Private Bills
position of the Canadian government is as stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on a number of occasions, namely that the Canadian government believes that it is not in the interests of the present generation that these tests be resumed, whether or not there is a system of control agreed on.
On other occasions I thought the view stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was unequivocal, but that the position taken by the government through the Prime Minister was equivocal. The statement made by the Prime Minister to a gathering last week in Montreal was to the effect that Canada favoured no resumption of tests, whether or not there was an agreement with the Soviet union. Notwithstanding what may have been achieved by the Soviet union as a result of the explosions of last fall, the view of the government of Canada is that there should not be any resumption of tests by the United States. This is a matter of vital importance. I take it that this is the policy of the government of Canada.

PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-42, to provide for minimum wages for employees.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a relatively simple bill and is applicable to a very small number of employees; in fact, it applies only to employees under the jurisdiction of federal fields of endeavour. It covers persons involved in such undertakings as the operation of ships, transportation by ships in Canada, maritime fields, telegraph, railway transportation, aerodromes, broadcasting, banking and such other works within the provinces as come under the general statutes of the federal government.
Therefore the number of employees who would be affected by this bill is limited. This problem has affected all the provinces and the federal government because of the very nature of our constitution. The British North America Act has the capacity of a constitution which makes it mandatory for the Canadian government to have limited legislation and federal jurisdiction over these people. Each of the provinces has its own jurisdiction of a similar nature where that jurisdiction applies. We are asking in this bill only for a basic minimum of $1.25 an hour.
Many members have asked me in the last few weeks if I did not feel that $1.25 an hour was a ridiculously low figure, particularly when the prevailing rates applying to most contracts handled by the federal government where day to day workers are employed is set at a level higher than the minimum for which we are asking here. However, we feel there should be a minimum rate and that it should not be a detrimental hiring rate in areas where industry will be following the lead given by the federal minimum wages. We feel that in some cases employers who are not favourable to establishing reasonable rates

and who often use the minimum rate as their maximum rate also will be influenced by this.
According to a review undertaken by the legislative branch of the Department of Labour, all the provinces now have minimum wage laws in operation. Prince Edward Island was the last province to enact such legislation. In the province of Ontario we have to date a minimum wage law affecting women only and the amount varies according to the zones in which they work. There are minimum wages in some of the provinces which are set as low as 44 cents an hour for workers under the age of 18. Unfortunately, most of the provincial legislation regarding minimum wages has set rates which are ridiculously low, and even those rates have been criticized by some employers because it was maintained that they did harm to their hiring rates.
We are introducing this measure in the hope that this legislation will give leadership to the provinces and encourage them to enact laws providing for a minimum rate as high as this minimum is. In Ontario the minimum rate for women is disgracefully low and that is true with regard to most of the other provinces. It is true that $1.25 is a very low figure in most areas in which the federal government is hiring people at a minimum rate of $1.65. In Port Arthur and the surrounding area I understand the rate is $1.85. However, our figure is considerably higher than the provincial prevailing rate in Ontario and in many other provinces.
We hope the minimum rate set out here will be taken as such. We hope it will protect workers in areas where abuses might otherwise take place, but that it will not necessarily be considered an acceptable rate for any particular area. It will be something to work from.
Some of the Conservative members on the eve of an election would probably like to refer to the fact that in 1935 Mr. R. B. Bennett, a former prime minister of this country, introduced legislation which would have provided certain minimum labour conditions in accordance with a labour code in keeping with the recommendations of the Geneva labour convention at that time. However, the legislation was ruled ultra vires under the terms of the British North America Act. Since that time very little federal labour legislation has been enacted of a kind which would give leadership to the provinces in this field. Considerable discussion could take place as to the reasons why it has been necessary to establish minimum wages and regulate working conditions in the provincial as well as the federal field. It might also be interesting to consider why the federal government has not developed a federal labour code of which a minimum wage would be part, so as to give 26207-1-189
Industrial Relations
leadership to the various provincial departments of labour across the country. This was the wish of Mr. R. B. Bennett in 1935. It is still, in my opinion, the wish of most labour organizations, of most employers organizations and also, I think, of this country in general, that we should find a way of putting into effect the recommendations which have been made over the years by the Geneva conventions as a means of protecting the rights of those in the labour field who are not in a position to bargain for themselves.
Of course, there are no unions across the country which would be asking for a minimum in the fields in which the federal government has jurisdiction; but an act such as we propose would give the leadership for which this country has been looking for many years. The present Minister of Labour is concerned with this matter and he has shown an understanding of the need for a national labour code, as well as of the need for improvement in many of the aspects of labour legislation. In addition, the government over the years has endorsed the decisions of the Geneva conventions affecting labour; so perhaps there has been an indication from Canada that there is a desire to see at least a basic federal labour code established which would include among other things a minimum wage for all employees.
Before I sit down I should like to point out that while we are debating a proposal for a minimum wage we would certainly wish to protect those rights which are enjoyed by employees, and that we would not wish the provision of a minimum wage to take away from any employee under federal jurisdiction any of the rights he now possesses.

subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
The
hon. member who introduced this measure stated that it is a simple bill. It is not too simple. It contains 19 clauses and some 50 subclauses. However, the principle of the bill is simple. It is to set a realistic minimum wage and I think that is a principle of which most members of this house will approve.
I thank the hon. member for having given credit to a former Conservative prime minister, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, for having introduced in his new deal legislation in 1935 the principle of a minimum wage. This was referred to when this bill was first introduced in this house, I believe on November 28, 1957, by Mr. Stanley Knowles. As far as I can make out, the only difference between this bill and the bill introduced by Mr. Knowles is that Mr. Knowles' bill set one dollar an hour as the minimum wage whereas this bill sets a rate of $1.25.
In the debate on the bill in 1957 as reported at page 1619 of Hansard, Mr. Knowles went on to point out that the Bennett proposal had

Industrial Relations
been ruled ultra vires in that it had been established by the courts by that time that labour-management matters came in part under federal jurisdiction and in part under provincial jurisdiction and therefore it was not competent for the federal parliament to pass a minimum wage act applicable to all wage earners in Canada. As reported at page 1619 of Hansard of November 28, 1957, Mr. Knowles went on to say:
I think it is fair to say that Mr. Bennett, the eminent lawyer that he was, knew of this difficulty and he tried to meet it by a rather lengthy and interesting preamble which can be found in chapter 44 of the statutes of 1935. The gist of that preamble was that Canada, having agreed to an international convention regarding the establishment of certain labour standards, including minimum wages, was obligated by that treaty arrangement to put such legislation on the statute books of the country.
Nevertheless that was not supported by the courts. This bill, dealing only with labour coming under federal jurisdiction, certainly is one with which parliament can deal. In previous debates the objection was raised that bills of this nature are money bills representing increased costs to the federal government. That argument cannot be sustained. I refer again to Mr. Knowles' statement on this question as reported at page 1623 of the date to which I have referred:
A bill, which does not involve a direct expenditure but merely confers upon the government a power for the exercise of which public money will have to be voted by parliament, is not a money bill and no resolution is necessary as a condition precedent to its introduction.
Those are not the words of Mr. Knowles. He was citing the headnote of a decision which appears at page 457 of Beauchesne's third edition.
In other words, if parliament passes this bill the costs, if there are any increased costs as a result of its passage, would still have to be approved by parliament when the estimates are considered.
As the sponsor of this bill said in his opening remarks the rate established by the bill of $1.25 an hour is much less than the rate set through collective bargaining negotiations with the various labour bodies who speak for practically all federal government workers in regard to wages. If this bill passes I am concerned that in some areas the minimum might become the maximum, which certainly would not be a very good thing.
There is a minimum wage law in the United States. I believe a proposal is currently being discussed to establish there a minimum wage of $1.25, which seems to be a reasonable figure although it is considerably above what Mr. Knowles in 1957 thought was reasonable.
I was interested in checking the rates specified in similar acts in the various provinces.

I cannot resist pointing out that in Saskatchewan, where one would think the thinking would be akin to that of the hon. member, the minimum wage is $30 a week for cities and the 15 larger towns within a five mile radius and $29 a week for the rest of the province. This applies to workers over 18 years of age. For those under age 18 the minimum is $2 less; that is, $28 in the larger towns and $27 in the rest of the province. This works out to something in the neighbourhood of 75 cents an hour, or if you wish to take the lower figure of $28 for someone under age 18 who is not employed in the 15 larger towns and cities it is 70 cents an hour. I am wondering why it is that that minimum wage level has been adopted by a province that has a government which is supposed to be a leader in social legislation.
As I said, the minimum wage was first introduced in parliament by a Conservative government, just as a Conservative government introduced hospital insurance, unemployment insurance and other legislation of benefit to the people of Canada. Therefore, there is nothing in the philosophy of this bill that a member on the government side would not consider worthy of consideration.
When we reach a clause by clause consideration of the bill various questions may arise. In some clauses of the bill the hon. member has gone a little far afield. I do not wish to discuss in detail the clauses of the bill but the hon. gentleman set specific limits on board and lodging. I am wondering whether those limits are the same in cases where the employer pays more than the minimum wage. I wonder whether the hon. member intends to set a rate of 50 cents for a meal and 75 cents for lodging in cases where the employer is paying as high as $2.50 an hour for labour. The provisions of the bill are vague in some respects and unrealistic in the light of present day costs, and these matters would have to be discussed when we reach detailed consideration of the bill.
The bill covers all federal employees. As I have said, most of these are fully covered by union agreements arranged through collective bargaining between the employer and the employee. I think of employees such as those engaged on railways, air lines and in communications. In paragraph (g) of clause 3 of the bill reference is made to employment in banks and banking. I am wondering whether employees in this field should be included in a measure of this kind. Questions of this sort would have to be examined by any committee considering the bill.
The hon. member proposes that records must be kept. I do not know the background

Industrial Relations
of this recommendation but the records proposed appear rather elaborate and would, I fear, become onerous. Perhaps modification is required here.
The hon. member has said this is a simple bill to provide a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour. I agree it is simple in its basic philosophy but not in any other respect. Before this bill was passed by parliament it would have to be thoroughly examined in committee. I am wondering, on the basis of indications in the last week, whether there would be sufficient time for the bill to receive the intensive checking in committee that would be necessary. I am in general agreement with the concept behind the bill but feel it requires thorough examination. I suppose the banking and commerce committee would be the appropriate place to which to refer the bill so that representatives of industry and labour could appear before the committee and state their views.
