Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Timiskaming is to be congratulated at least on his tenacity, for this bill has the look of an old friend. We have heard a good deal about it in the last few years. I should like to say that I am quite sure that, regardless of where he sits, every member of this house will subscribe to the principle that the worker is 26207-1-189J
worthy of his hire. Underlying the presentation of this bill I presume there is that wish to see that the worker receives due reward for the energy he expends. Yet at the same time I find it very hard to reconcile certain statements made by the hon. member who introduced this bill, and certain phases of the bill, with the progress that my hon. friend hopes may be made when the bill is passed.
I am particularly concerned at the moment with clause 2(b) which states that "employee" means a person of any age. It is conceivable that in certain departments or in certain avenues of work juniors would be preferable. I can think of a great many young persons in my own community to whom I certainly would not wish to pay $1.25 an hour. Mention was made of the fact that in one area the minimum wage is 48 cents an hour. I am not saying that is a proper wage. However, I believe that we are imposing a handicap when we say to any employer, "You will pay $1.25 an hour for labour regardless of sex and regardless of age". A young man, possibly of the age of 16 years, having left school and receiving $1.25 an hour for a seven hour day, would receive $8.75 a day. If he worked five days a week he would receive $43.75. That amount may not appear to be excessive. Perhaps it is not excessive. However, I say that it represents a figure which may be out of balance with the wages received by the older person. A young man 25 years of age I think would automatically consider that, if his younger brother of fifteen years or sixteen years can receive $43.75 a week, he is being underpaid at $60 or $65. I find it extremely difficult to embrace this bill in the broad terms in which it has been outlined.
A moment ago I said that the worker is worthy of his hire. We all subscribe to this principle. However, how does one determine worthiness? That point seems to be the key to the matter. If this provision was to apply to a specially trained group, a group with certain known qualifications, or if it was to apply to certain specialized work, there might be more justification for that particular clause than there is now. However, you cannot get qualification and you certainly cannot get experience in a young head and a young body. I believe there should be some amendment to this bill-and I am not going to propose it- which would take out of the bill itself this question of sex and age and which would put the bill on a firm basis with respect to the type of labour for which it is intended.
I agree with many of the things said by my colleague the hon. member who last spoke. We are in sympathy with this type of legislation. We wish to see the people of this country obtain a decent living. Regardless of where

Industrial Relations
we sit in the house, I am quite sure that all of us would applaud any forward looking step which would place the extremely low salaried worker-particularly the more adult worker -on a basis of comfort and equality consistent, of course, with services rendered. However, times change. I can remember, Mr. Chairman, when my father came to this country in the early part of this century, when I was a very small boy. He worked for a dollar a day and he was glad to be able to work. I myself can remember working for 50 cents a day and working long hours. It is true that the dollar or the 50 cents meant a great deal more then than it does today. I will grant that fact. However, those were the days of competition for work. We were obliged to get out and find our own jobs. Many of us worked on farms in western Canada for $25 or $30 and our board a month, and we were the better for it as we learned that it was necessary for us to produce something in the way of constructive labour in order to enjoy the advantages of a wage at all.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with all kindness and with all respect for the mover of this bill I say that the hon. member might be well advised to take a second look at it and to bring into it some clarification as to the persons to whom it basically should apply.
I am sure there are many other members of the house who would like to speak on this bill. It is an important one. We are all interested in workers. Most of us are workers ourselves. I do not intend to monopolize the time of the house. In closing let me say this. Regardless of party, experience, or outlook and particularly regardless of economic position, I am sure there is not a man or lady in this house who will not endorse the basic principle of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to make any comments on this bill, even though it has been before this house in previous sessions. However, I have read the contributions of hon. members from all sides of the house in previous debates. The thing that struck me from the beginning was that while everyone is in agreement with the basic principle outlined in this bill, there may not be agreement as to the amount and there may not be agreement as to various clauses and subsections of the bill. The situation therefore is one in which everyone wishes to achieve the same end but differs as to the method of going about it.
Another thing that struck me was the need for the introduction of a bill like this. We all know from past history, of course, of instances in which labour was exploited by employers. We have come a long way since then. However, the fact that we have

a bill like this before us would indicate that there is still the isolated instance in this country where labour is being exploited. Coming as I do from the city of Winnipeg may I say this. We had there an experience about which I am sure all members of the house have heard and read. I am, of course, referring to the 1919 Winnipeg general strike. Following that strike the trade union movement grew up and bargained with employers for wages. I think the way our unions have conducted themselves in the past and are conducting themselves at the present time is a credit to Canadian labour. Personally I feel it is a pity that in some instances we do not have 100 per cent Canadian unions and that some of them are still controlled by our neighbour to the south. I also think it is a pity that in some cases there is apathy among some of the union members themselves so that power is concentrated in one or two at the top without in some instances the sanction of the rank and file. But by and large the history of unions in Canada and what they have accomplished for the workers of this country is very commendable indeed.
Previous speakers have pointed out that in this sprawling land of ours-and some consider it is a miracle that it has remained together as long as it has-our lines of geographical barriers run north and south and our economic lines run north and south. Across this country there are various standards of living and various bases of economic stability. Therefore what may be regarded as a minimum wage in accordance with the standard of living in one part of the country may be far too high in the light of the standard of living in another part of the country.
When one looks at the type of workers who would be covered by this kind of legislation he cannot help asking the question, is there a real need for a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour? I would be interested in the production of figures before a committee to which this bill might be referred, to determine the number of employees in these various categories who are in fact being paid less than $1.25 an hour; and if there should be a substantial number I would be interested in the category of work, the age and education of the employees in the various groups. In that regard I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Medicine Hat, who pointed out that there are types of work which would not require a wage of $1.25 an hour or whatever the figure might be.
I am also interested in the points that have been brought out with regard to the minimum wage legislation in the various provinces of this country. I would think that the result we

are seeking could probably be better achieved by working through the provinces, either through a provincial conference with respect to conformity of legislation or through the various labour groups approaching the province in which they are active and in which they are aware of the economic conditions and circumstances, the standard of living and all of the other factors that go into determining a principle such as this. I think it could probably be done better on a local provincial basis rather than through the House of Commons. That has been pointed out by previous speakers when they mentioned that legislation passed in 1935 was disallowed by the Supreme Court of Canada, and therefore we are confined to workers falling under federal jurisdiction.
The arguments I have tried to present and the arguments that others have presented indicate to me that while we want to achieve a certain result, a great deal of discussion must be done in committee on the various clauses of the bill. There is a great deal of information required and a great deal of time must be spent on the matter in order to achieve that result with which all members of the house will be in agreement. I commend the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) for introducing the bill and I hope that other members will express their views on it. I would be particularly interested in hearing from a member of the Liberal party, of whom there are few in the house this afternoon. I think they have something to offer as private members, as well as a party, and I would hope that before the hour ends we would hear from one of the two who are in the chamber this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, after this short interruption I should like to go ahead and say a few words about Bill No. C-42 introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming, which we are now discussing. In general terms I approve of the principle of a minimum wage law for federal employees. Historically I think one of the disgraces of our social system has been the unfair wages paid to those who offer their services. We can think back a good many years and realize that originally the worst exploitation was of child labour and of women who were employed in work that normally should have been done by men. But they were not the only victims of exploitation. For many years men have also been exploited in the services they have to offer to employers.
We know that out of this situation have arisen the labour unions in Canada, North America and throughout the world. I think no one will deny that the labour unions have done a great deal toward raising the standard of wages throughout the world and in that way they have served a very good and useful purpose. Prior to the time labour unions became strong enough to exert influence against employers who were oppressing workmen, it was difficult for anyone to buck the employers and the big corporations.
I think it is also fair to say that there are some people who now believe that perhaps the labour unions have at last reached the same level of power as management, or have perhaps gone beyond that and have overplayed their hand. This appeared to be the situation a few years ago, but I think it is now coming back to normal and there seems now to be a fair distribution in our social system between the powers of large corporations and those of the labour unions. We have just seen an instance this week in the neighbouring country to the south of the power that management is still able to wield. We do realize that it is necessary not only for the workers of the country but also for the government to maintain their strength at this particular moment.
In so far as this bill is concerned, I may say that for many years there have been technical problems in connection with the setting of minimum wages for federal employees. We can think back to the days of the late R. B. Bennett when there was an effort made to pass a minimum wage law for Canada. As hon. members know, this law was declared ultra vires of the federal parliament. I think the reason for this was made obvious in that the act was an effort to legislate in connection with wage standards across Canada. It became clear that this was beyond
2S78

Industrial Relations
the power of the parliament of Canada because it invaded a provincial sphere and for that reason the legislation was declared ultra vires.
However, I think this bill makes an effort to overcome that problem. I am not sure whether or not it accomplishes this purpose, but it certainly makes an effort to get around the difficulty because the effect of it purports to apply only to those who are federal employees or employees of corporations under the control of the federal government. It is very interesting to recall that when the minimum wage legislation was before the Supreme Court of Canada some 25 years ago, the supreme court divided evenly, three judges to three judges. One wonders why the court would have been so composed as to allow such a possibility, but apparently only six judges sat on the case and three felt it was ultra vires while three felt it was not. As a result, the legislation then went to the privy council which held that it was ultra vires and the legislation thereupon became ineffective.
The decision reached at that time is very interesting in view of the fact that the Supreme Court of Canada is now the final appeal body in Canada, and one could speculate as to what the decision of that court might be today in a similar case. A portion of the judgment which held that the legislation was intra vires reads as follows:
From two main considerations, the conclusion follows that legislative authority in respect of international agreements is, as regards Canada, vested exclusively in the parliament of Canada. First, by virtue of section 132 of the British North America Act, jurisdiction, legislative and executive, for the purpose of giving effect to any treaty obligation imposed upon Canada, or any one of the provinces of Canada, by force of a treaty between the British Empire and a foreign country, is committed to the parliament and government of Canada. This jurisdiction of the dominion the privy council held, in the aeronautics case and in the radio case is exclusive; and consequently, under the British North America Act, the provinces have no power and never had power to legislate for the purpose of giving effect to an international agreement: That, as a subject of legislation, is excluded from the jurisdiction envisaged by section 92.
There was a great deal more of the judgment that might be read. However, I believe it is fair to say that, as a result of the judgment, the legislation was abandoned.
In so far as Bill No. C-42 is concerned, I have looked at it carefully in an effort to see whether or not it does get around the difficulties that were inherent in the legislation declared ultra vires previously. There are one or two clauses that might be considered ultra vires. However, since it is not the custom on second reading to go into bills section by section, I would prefer not
[Mr. Aiken.l
to do so now. I merely say that the bill sets forth a useful purpose and is worthy of consideration. I would hope that the difficulties of the past in connection with wages would be met and that the government would eventually give consideration to this type of legislation.
